a: This is the family history of Jacob
p: The heading toledot, "generations," opens the last of the main sections of Genesis.
b: The Hebrew toledot, often translated "generations," heads each major section of Genesis (2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 11:27; 25:19; 36:1). It names the father, but the section tells the story of his children. So "the family history of Jacob" is mostly about Joseph and Judah, and it runs to the end of the book. Jacob is still alive and still central: the section closes with his blessing and burial (49–50).

a: Joseph brought their father a bad report about them
p: The text does not say whether the report was true. Readers have judged Joseph both ways.
b: The word dibbah usually means a damaging, often false, report (Numbers 13:32; Proverbs 10:18). The narrator does not say what the brothers did or whether Joseph exaggerated. Rashi, following the Midrash (Genesis Rabbah), says Joseph reported three faults and was later punished measure for measure for each: he was sold as a slave, his brothers dipped his robe in goat's blood, and he was tempted by Potiphar's wife. Many modern readers see a spoiled seventeen-year-old, and the story lets him grow up. Christian readers who see Joseph as a type of Christ tend to read the report as truthful witness against wrongdoing.

a: a robe that reached to his hands and feet
t: Not a coat of many colors
p: The Hebrew probably describes a long robe with sleeves, not a multicolored coat.
b: The phrase ketonet passim joins "tunic" with passim, a word that elsewhere means the flat of the hand or foot. The likely sense is a robe reaching to the wrists and ankles: clothing for someone who does not do field work. The only other use describes the robe of a king's unmarried daughter (2 Samuel 13:18–19). "Coat of many colors" comes from the Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus), which has chitōna poikilon, "a many-colored tunic," and from the KJV. E. A. Speiser compared an Akkadian term for an ornamented garment. Either way, the robe marks Joseph as the favored heir.

a: the son of his old age
t: Son of his old age, or a wise son?
p: Benjamin was younger, so the rabbis and the Targum read the phrase as "a wise son."
b: Joseph was not Jacob's youngest son; Benjamin was born later (35:18). Most commentators answer that Joseph was the first son of Jacob's old age, and the firstborn of his beloved Rachel (30:22–24). Targum Onkelos, the standard Aramaic translation read in synagogues, renders it "a wise son," taking zequnim (old age) in the sense of zaqen, "elder," a man of wisdom. Rashi adds that Jacob taught Joseph everything he had learned.

a: my bundle got up and stood upright
p: Sheaves and stars: both dreams show the family bowing to Joseph, and the first hints at grain.
b: The first dream is set at harvest and the second in the sky, but both end with bowing. The grain fits what will happen: the brothers will bow to Joseph when they come to buy grain (42:6; 43:26; 44:14). In Genesis a dream that comes twice means the matter is settled (41:32), and Joseph has two dreams here, as the cupbearer and the baker will have a pair of dreams between them, and Pharaoh two of his own. Notice that Joseph's dreams have no interpreter. Everyone, including Joseph, understands them at once.

a: I and your mother and your brothers
p: Rachel had already died (35:19). Readers explain the "mother" in the dream in several ways.
b: Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin (35:19), yet Jacob speaks as if she were alive. Some critical scholars think this story once stood in a tradition in which Rachel was still living. Rashi, following Genesis Rabbah, has Jacob argue that the dream cannot be literal, since Rachel is dead; others in the Midrash say the mother is Bilhah, who raised Joseph. A literary reading notes that dreams in Genesis are not always fulfilled in every detail: Jacob himself never clearly bows to Joseph (but see the note at 47:31). Revelation 12:1 borrows the sun, moon and twelve stars for its picture of the people of God.

a: his father held on to what he had said
p: Jacob scolds Joseph but quietly remembers the dream, much as Mary does in Luke.
b: The verb shamar, "keep, guard," here means to hold something in memory and wait to see what comes of it (compare Daniel 7:28). Luke uses the same idea for Mary, who "kept all these things, turning them over in her heart" (Luke 2:19, 51). Jacob's public rebuke and private attention set up the long wait before the dream comes true.

a: from the valley of Hebron
p: Joseph walked about 50 miles north from Hebron to Shechem and then about 15 more to Dothan.
b: Hebron sits in the hills of Judah, about 20 miles south of Jerusalem; Shechem lies near modern Nablus, about 50 miles north of Hebron (some 30 miles north of Jerusalem); Dothan is about 15 miles beyond that, on the route from the hills toward the coast. Jacob's sons had a history at Shechem (34:25–30), which may explain Jacob's worry. Hebron is high ground, so "valley" puzzled the rabbis. Rashi reads it as a hint at "the deep counsel" of Abraham, who is buried at Hebron: God's word to him that his offspring would be strangers in a land not theirs (15:13).

a: A man came upon him
t: Who was the man in the field?
p: An unnamed stranger points Joseph to Dothan. The rabbis said he was an angel.
b: Without this nameless stranger, Joseph would have gone home and the story would have stopped. The Midrash and Rashi identify him as the angel Gabriel, and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan says the same. Modern readers see the narrator's quiet way of showing that events are being guided: the Joseph story almost never shows God acting openly, yet small "chances" keep moving Joseph toward Egypt. Compare the unnamed man who wrestles with Jacob (32:24).

a: Let's head for Dothan
p: Dothan was a real town on a trade route, which is why a caravan passed by.
b: Tell Dothan, north of Shechem, was excavated by Joseph Free from 1953 to 1964 and was occupied in the Bronze and Iron Ages. It lay on a road from Gilead and the Jezreel Valley down to the coast and on to Egypt, the route the Ishmaelite caravan takes in 37:25. Later the prophet Elisha was surrounded by an Aramean army at Dothan (2 Kings 6:13–17).

a: that master dreamer
p: The brothers' sneer is literally "the master of dreams."
b: Ba'al hachalomot means "the owner" or "master of the dreams." Hebrew uses ba'al plus a noun for a person marked by something ("master of hair" for a hairy man, 2 Kings 1:8). In the brothers' mouth it is mockery: "His Highness the Dreamer." The irony is that he does become master of dreams, the one man in Egypt who can explain them (41:15).

a: But Reuben heard, and he saved him from them
p: The firstborn tries to save Joseph but never confronts his brothers openly.
b: Reuben, the oldest, plans to come back and return Joseph to their father (37:22). Some readers think he wants to win back Jacob's favor after sleeping with Bilhah (35:22). His plan fails because he is away when the sale happens (37:29). Reuben's good intentions without follow-through recur in 42:22 and 42:37, and they contrast with Judah, who first proposes the sale (37:26–27) but later puts his own life on the line (43:9; 44:33). Some source critics think Reuben and Judah were heroes of two different versions of this story (see the note at 37:28).

a: It was a dry pit, with no water in it
p: The "pit" was a cistern, a dry hole cut in rock to store rainwater.
b: The Hebrew bor is a bottle-shaped cistern cut into rock to collect winter rain. Empty in the dry season, it made an inescapable prison. Jeremiah was later held in one with mud at the bottom (Jeremiah 38:6). The same word is used for Joseph's prison in Egypt (40:15; 41:14), tying the two low points of his life together. The Talmud (Shabbat 22a) says that although there was no water, there were snakes and scorpions.

a: Then they sat down to eat their meal
p: The brothers eat while Joseph pleads below, a scene later prophets and rabbis remembered.
b: Only later do we learn that Joseph begged them from the pit (42:21). The prophet Amos condemns the comfortable rich who "drink wine by the bowlful ... but the ruin of Joseph does not make them sick" (Amos 6:6), where "Joseph" means the northern tribes, but the picture fits this scene. The meal also anticipates the feast at which the brothers later eat in Joseph's house, still not knowing who he is (43:31–34).

a: their camels carrying gum, balm and myrrh
p: Gum, balm and resin: luxury goods carried from Gilead to Egypt.
b: The three products are nekot (probably gum tragacanth), tsori (balm, a healing resin; compare "Is there no balm in Gilead?" Jeremiah 8:22), and lot, which is not true myrrh but probably ladanum, a fragrant resin from the rockrose. Egypt used such resins in medicine, perfume and embalming. Jacob later sends the same products to Egypt as a gift (43:11). On camels in the ancestor stories, see 12:16 and 24:10.

a: What is the profit if we kill our brother and hide his blood?
p: Judah's question looks back to Cain and Abel. Blood that is covered still cries out.
b: Genesis has already said that a brother's blood cries out from the ground (4:10), and Job prays, "Earth, do not cover my blood" (Job 16:18; compare Ezekiel 24:7–8). Judah's argument is practical rather than moral: murder brings no gain. Still, it saves Joseph's life. Judah's word for "profit," betsa', often means dishonest gain (Exodus 18:21).

a: Then Midianite traders passed by
t: Midianites or Ishmaelites? Who sold Joseph?
p: Verses 25–36 name both Ishmaelites and Midianites. Readers explain this in three main ways.
b: One group, two names. Judges 8:24 calls Midianites "Ishmaelites," so "Ishmaelite" may mean caravan traders in general (Kitchen, Wenham). Two groups. Rashbam, the 12th-century French Jewish commentator, read the verse so that the Midianites pulled Joseph out while the brothers were eating, and sold him without the brothers knowing; Rashi has Joseph sold several times. This would explain Reuben's shock (37:29) and the brothers' later claim that Joseph begged "us" (42:21) without saying they sold him; but Joseph says "you sold me" (45:4). Two sources. Many critical scholars see two versions woven together: in one, Judah's plan and Ishmaelites; in the other, Reuben's plan and Midianites (see 39:1 and 37:36).

a: twenty pieces of silver
p: Twenty shekels fits slave prices of the early second millennium BC, and later Israel's law.
b: "Pieces" are shekels, a weight of about 11 grams. Kenneth Kitchen argues that 20 shekels matches the average price of a slave in Old Babylonian texts (about 1800–1600 BC), while later prices rose to about 30 shekels and in the first millennium to 50 or more. Critical scholars such as Donald Redford and Claus Westermann reply that slave prices varied widely by place and period, so the figure cannot date the story; some also compare Leviticus 27:5, which values a male aged five to twenty at twenty shekels. The Septuagint makes the price twenty pieces of gold (see the variant). Christian readers have long compared Judah's sale of Joseph with Judas (the same name in Greek) selling Jesus for thirty pieces (Matthew 26:15; Zechariah 11:12).

a: killed a male goat, and soaked the robe in the blood
p: Jacob once fooled his father with a goat and a brother's clothes. Now his sons fool him the same way.
b: To steal Esau's blessing, Jacob served Isaac two young goats and wore Esau's clothes and goatskins (27:9, 15–16). Now Jacob's sons use a goat and a brother's garment to deceive him. Judah will be paid back in the same coin in the next chapter, when he sends a young goat (38:17, 20) and is confronted with his own belongings. The story never states the moral; it lets the repetition speak.

a: Please look closely
p: The brothers' words, haker na, return word for word when Tamar confronts Judah (38:25).
b: Haker na means "please examine, identify." The same two words come back when Tamar sends Judah his seal and staff (38:25), and the verb nakar runs through the whole story: Isaac failed to recognize Jacob (27:23), and Joseph will recognize his brothers while they do not recognize him (42:7–8). The Midrash Genesis Rabbah draws the link: God says to Judah, "You said to your father, 'Recognize, please.' By your life, Tamar will say to you, 'Recognize, please.'" Robert Alter made this pairing a classic example of how biblical stories comment on each other.

a: I will go down to my son in Sheol
p: This is the first time the Bible names Sheol, the shadowy place of the dead.
b: Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as deep under the earth, where all the dead go, good and bad alike (Psalm 89:48; Ecclesiastes 9:10). It is not the same as the later idea of hell. The KJV here translates it "the grave" and elsewhere "hell" or "the pit," which hides that one word is used. Jacob uses it again three times (42:38; 44:29, 31). Later passages begin to hope that God will rescue from Sheol (Psalm 16:10; 49:15), and Acts 2:27 applies Psalm 16 to Jesus' resurrection.

a: to Potiphar, a court official of Pharaoh
p: His name is Egyptian, "the one whom Ra gave." Its form helps scholars argue about dates.
b: Potiphar (and Potiphera in 41:45) matches the Egyptian Pa-di-pa-Ra, "the one whom Ra [the sun god] gave." Names built on the pattern "the one whom god X gave" are common from about 1000 BC on and especially in the 600s–500s BC. Donald Redford took this as evidence that the story was written late; Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier reply that the pattern has earlier forms and that a later scribe may have updated a name. The word for "official," saris, can mean "eunuch," but it is also a general title for a court officer, and Potiphar has a wife.

a: About that time Judah went down, away from his brothers
t: Why does Judah's story interrupt Joseph's?
p: Chapter 38 breaks into the Joseph story. Some see a clumsy insertion, others a deliberate mirror.
b: Joseph has just been sold (37:36), and his story resumes only in 39:1. Many critical scholars (Gunkel, von Rad, Westermann) see chapter 38 as an independent tradition about the tribe of Judah placed here without much regard for the plot. Literary readers, following Robert Alter and Umberto Cassuto, see careful design: Judah "goes down" just as Joseph is "taken down" (39:1); the goat and "recognize, please" repeat from 37:31–33; and Judah's failure with Tamar sets up his change in chapters 43–44. The timing is also a puzzle: Judah's grandsons go down to Egypt in 46:12 only about 22 years later. Ibn Ezra suggested that the chapter starts before Joseph's sale.

a: the daughter of a Canaanite man whose name was Shua
p: Abraham and Isaac refused Canaanite wives for their sons. Judah takes one without comment.
b: Abraham made his servant swear not to take a Canaanite wife for Isaac (24:3), and Isaac and Rebekah sent Jacob away to avoid one (27:46–28:1). Judah marries a Canaanite and the narrator does not condemn him, though his first two sons come to bad ends. She is never named; she is only "the daughter of Shua" (38:12; 1 Chronicles 2:3 calls her "Bath-shua," which means the same). The rabbis, uneasy, sometimes read "Canaanite" as "merchant" (as in Proverbs 31:24; Targum Onkelos and Rashi).

a: Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil
p: Er's name spelled backward is the Hebrew word for "evil."
b: In Hebrew, Er is 'er (ער) and "evil" is ra' (רע): the same two letters reversed. The narrator does not say what Er did. This is also the first time in the Bible that the LORD is said to put a particular person to death. The rabbis guessed that Er, like Onan, avoided having children (Genesis Rabbah; Talmud Yevamot 34b).

a: Do a brother-in-law's duty to her
p: When a man died childless, his brother was expected to father a son in the dead man's name.
b: The verb yabam means to act as a yabam, a husband's brother. The custom, later written into the Law (Deuteronomy 25:5–10), let a man who died without a son still have an heir: the first son of his widow and his brother counted as the dead man's and inherited his share. Similar customs are known from Hittite and Middle Assyrian laws. The widow was protected, the family land stayed in the family, and the dead man's "name" lived on. Ruth 4 is the other great biblical story built on this custom, and it looks back to this one (Ruth 4:12).

a: he spilled his seed on the ground
p: The text condemns Onan for refusing his brother an heir. Later debates used the verse for other purposes.
b: The verse explains the motive: Onan "knew that the children would not count as his," so he used his brother's widow while refusing to give her a son. He would also inherit more if Er had no heir. The sin, in context, is selfish cheating of a widow and a dead brother. The word "onanism" later came to mean masturbation, which is not described here. The Talmud (Niddah 13a) used the verse against wasting seed, and Augustine and later Catholic teaching (for example Pius XI's Casti Connubii, 1930) cited it against contraception. Most modern commentators, Jewish and Christian, read it as about the levirate duty, while some still see a wider principle.
orig: וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה (veshichet artsah), "and he ruined [it] on the ground"

a: Or he too will die, like his brothers
p: Judah seems to think Tamar is a deadly wife, and he quietly leaves her in limbo.
b: The narrator lets us hear Judah's private reason: he fears that Tamar is somehow to blame for his sons' deaths. Later Jewish tradition knew the idea of a "killer wife" (the book of Tobit tells of a woman whose seven husbands died, Tobit 3:8). By sending Tamar back to her father, Judah leaves her bound to his family but with no husband and no child, unable to remarry. Verse 14 confirms that he never intended to keep his promise.

a: sat at the gateway of Enaim
p: Enaim means "two springs" or "two eyes": Tamar waits at the place called Eye-Opening.
b: Petach Enayim can be a place name, "the gateway of Enaim" (perhaps the Enam of Joshua 15:34, in Judah's hills), but it also reads "the opening of the eyes." Judah's eyes are about to be opened. The Talmud (Sotah 10a) and the Targums played on the double meaning. Some older translations, including the KJV ("an open place"), took it as a description rather than a name.

a: he took her for a prostitute, because she had covered her face
p: The text says Judah took her for a prostitute because her face was covered. Veils had more than one meaning.
b: A Middle Assyrian law (Tablet A, law 40) required married women to be veiled in public and forbade prostitutes to veil. If customs in Canaan were similar, a veil would not mark a prostitute. Many scholars think the point is simply that her face was hidden, so Judah did not know her, and that a woman sitting alone at a roadside was assumed to be selling herself. Rebekah veiled herself before meeting Isaac (24:65), a bride's gesture.

a: Your seal and your cord, and your staff
p: A seal on a cord and a carved staff were a man's personal marks, like a signature and an ID card.
b: The seal was probably a cylinder or stamp seal, worn on a cord around the neck, used to sign clay documents. The staff likely had a carved top that made it recognizable. Herodotus says that every Babylonian man carried a seal and a carved staff (Histories 1.195). Tamar asks for the things that prove identity beyond doubt. Judah, the leader, hands over his authority for a moment's pleasure; Judah's "staff" returns as a royal symbol in 49:10.

a: Where is the holy woman
p: Hirah politely uses qedeshah, "consecrated woman," not the plain word for prostitute.
b: The narrator and Judah say zonah, "prostitute" (38:15, 24). Hirah, asking in public, says qedeshah, literally "holy" or "set-apart woman." Older scholarship translated it "temple prostitute" (the NIV has "shrine prostitute"), assuming that Canaanite religion practiced sacred sex. Joan Westenholz and others have shown that the evidence for ritual prostitution in the ancient Near East is thin; a qadishtu in Mesopotamia was a cultic woman who could serve as a midwife or wet nurse. Hirah may simply be using a more respectable word. Deuteronomy 23:17–18 later bans both the qedeshah and the zonah in Israel.

a: let her be burned
p: Judah, head of the clan, orders the harshest death for a pregnancy that might be his own.
b: Tamar was still bound to Judah's family as Shelah's promised wife, so her pregnancy counted as adultery. As head of the family, Judah could judge. Burning was the law's penalty for a priest's daughter who became a prostitute (Leviticus 21:9) and for certain incest (Leviticus 20:14); ordinary adultery called for stoning (Deuteronomy 22:21–24). The command shows Judah at his worst, quick to condemn the woman he wronged, about to be judged by his own seal and staff.

a: While they were bringing her out, she sent a message to her father-in-law
p: The Talmud praises Tamar for letting Judah confess instead of exposing him publicly.
b: Tamar does not name Judah. She sends his things privately with a question, leaving him free to stay silent and let her die. The Talmud (Sotah 10b) draws a famous lesson: "It is better for a person to throw himself into a fiery furnace than to shame his fellow in public." The link between Judah's confession and his tribe's kingship is drawn elsewhere: Genesis Rabbah 99:8, the Tosefta (Berakhot 4:18), and Targum Onkelos on 49:8, "Judah, you confessed and were not ashamed." Tamar's question repeats the brothers' words to Jacob, "Please look closely" (see 37:32).

a: She is more in the right than I am
p: Judah's confession is his turning point, and the first step toward his speech in chapter 44.
b: Tsadqah mimmenni can mean "She is more righteous than I" or "She is in the right, not I." Tsedeq here is not general moral goodness but being in the right in this case: Tamar acted to secure the child owed to her husband's line, and Judah had blocked it. Ruth 4:12 blesses Boaz's house "like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah," and Matthew names Tamar first of the four women in Jesus' family tree (Matthew 1:3). The Talmud reads mimmenni also as a heavenly voice saying "From me came these things" (Sotah 10b).

a: tied a scarlet thread around it
p: As with Jacob and Esau, the twins struggle at birth and the younger comes out ahead.
b: Rebekah's twins also struggled, with Jacob grasping Esau's heel (25:24–26). Here the boy marked as firstborn is overtaken by his brother, as younger sons keep overtaking older ones in Genesis (Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Ephraim). Perez becomes the ancestor of Boaz and David (Ruth 4:18–22; 1 Chronicles 2:4–15). Some Christian writers linked the scarlet thread with Rahab's scarlet cord (Joshua 2:18) as a sign of salvation; that link is a later reading, not something the text says.

a: What a breach you have made for yourself!
p: Perez means "breaking through." The name fits a line that breaks through to the throne.
b: Parats means to break out or burst through. The midwife's cry names the child Perez, "Breach." Zerah (38:30) sounds like zarach, "to shine" or "dawn," perhaps for the bright scarlet thread. Later, David's ancestry runs through Perez (Ruth 4:18), and the verb returns in God's "breaking out" for David (2 Samuel 5:20; 6:8).

a: Joseph, meanwhile, had been brought down to Egypt
p: Egyptian records show many people from Canaan living and working in Egypt, some rising high.
b: Egyptian texts and pictures from the Middle and New Kingdoms show "Asiatics" (people from Canaan and Syria) as traders, slaves, soldiers and household servants. A papyrus now in the Brooklyn Museum (from the 1700s BC) lists dozens of Asiatic household servants with Semitic names. Manfred Bietak's excavations at Tell el-Dab'a (ancient Avaris) in the eastern Nile Delta uncovered a large Canaanite population there in the 1800s–1500s BC. Some foreigners reached high office, such as Aper-El, a vizier with a Semitic name in the 1300s BC. None of this proves the Joseph story, but it shows the setting is realistic.

a: The LORD was with Joseph
p: Chapter 39 uses the name YHWH eight times. Most of the Joseph story says only "God."
b: Outside chapters 38–39 and 49:18, the narrator and characters in chapters 37–50 say Elohim, "God," and never the personal name YHWH (printed "the LORD"). Here the narrator frames Joseph's slavery and prison with "the LORD was with him" (39:2, 3, 21, 23), while Joseph, speaking to an Egyptian, says "God" (39:9). Source critics assign this chapter to the J source, which uses YHWH. Literary readers point out that the narrator uses the covenant name when telling the reader what is really going on, and "God" when characters speak to foreigners. "With" is the key word: God was "with" Isaac and Jacob too (26:3; 28:15).

a: the LORD began to bless the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake
p: God promised Abraham that the nations would be blessed through his family. Here it begins in Egypt.
b: God promised that in Abraham "all the families of the earth will be blessed" (12:3; repeated to Jacob in 28:14). Laban admitted he had been blessed because of Jacob (30:27). Now an Egyptian household prospers because of Joseph, and later all Egypt will survive the famine through him (41:57; 47:25). Joseph is the clearest picture in Genesis of how Abraham's family was meant to bless the world.

a: the food on his plate
p: Probably plain fact, or a hint at Egyptian food laws. Rashi read it as a polite way to say "his wife."
b: On the surface Potiphar trusts Joseph with everything and thinks only about his meals. Some scholars connect this with 43:32: Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews, so Potiphar kept his food in Egyptian hands. Rashi, following the Midrash (Genesis Rabbah), took "food" as a polite word for Potiphar's wife, matching Joseph's words in 39:9: "he has kept nothing back from me except you." Either way, the next line turns at once to Joseph's good looks.

a: Joseph had a fine build and good looks
p: The same words describe Rachel (29:17). In Hebrew stories good looks often bring danger.
b: Yefeh to'ar viyfeh mar'eh, "beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance," is exactly what Genesis says of Joseph's mother Rachel (29:17). Few men are described this way in the Bible: David (1 Samuel 16:12, 17:42) and Absalom (2 Samuel 14:25). Beauty draws trouble: Sarah in Egypt (12:11–15), Rebekah (26:7), Tamar daughter of David (2 Samuel 13:1). Jewish and Muslim tradition made Joseph the model of male beauty; the Qur'an tells of Egyptian women who cut their hands when they saw him (Surah 12:31).

a: sin against God
p: Joseph gives two reasons: loyalty to his master and fear of God.
b: Joseph's answer is the longest speech he makes in this chapter. First, it would betray a master who trusted him with everything. Second, it would be a "great evil" and "sin against God." Adultery is called a "great sin" also in Egyptian and other ancient Near Eastern marriage texts, and in Abimelech's words (20:9). Jewish tradition calls Joseph ha-tsaddiq, "the righteous," mainly for this refusal. The Talmud (Sotah 36b) says he was on the edge of giving in when he saw the image of his father's face in the window (see 39:11). Christian writers from Ambrose (On Joseph) on held him up as a model of chastity.

a: he went indoors to do his work
p: The Talmud records a debate: did Joseph go in to work, or to give in?
b: "To do his work" is plain enough, but the empty house invites a question. In the Talmud (Sotah 36b), Rav and Shmuel disagree: one says he went to do his actual work, the other that he went in intending to sin, and was stopped when he saw a vision of his father Jacob. The same passage reads 49:24, "his bow stayed steady," as a hint of this scene. The Bible itself says only that Joseph refused and ran. Hebrews 4:15 says Jesus was "tested in all things, in the same way we are, but apart from sin," a line Christians have often linked with Joseph.

a: he left his garment in her hand and ran outside
p: Once again Joseph's clothes are used as false evidence against him.
b: Clothing runs through Joseph's story. His brothers strip his robe and use it to prove a lie (37:23, 31–33). Now Potiphar's wife holds his garment as "proof" of a lie (39:16–18). Later he is given new clothes to stand before Pharaoh (41:14) and robes of fine linen as ruler (41:42), and he gives clothes to his brothers (45:22). Tamar's change of clothes in chapter 38 belongs to the same pattern. Each change of clothing marks a change in Joseph's status.

a: He brought us a Hebrew to toy with us
p: She turns the servants against a foreign slave, and her word for "toy with" has a double edge.
b: "Hebrew" is the word outsiders use for Abraham's family (14:13; 41:12; Exodus 1:15–16). By saying "he has brought us a Hebrew," she blames her husband and makes the servants' honor the issue. The verb tsachaq means "to laugh, to play," and in some contexts "to fondle" (26:8, where Isaac is "laughing" with Rebekah). It is the root of Isaac's name. So "to toy with us" can mean both mockery and sexual advances.

a: That Hebrew servant you brought into our house came in to me
p: An Egyptian story about 1200 BC has a similar plot: a wife's false accusation against a young man.
b: In the Egyptian Tale of Two Brothers (Papyrus d'Orbiney, about 1200 BC), the wife of Anubis tries to seduce his younger brother Bata. When he refuses, she pretends he attacked her, and Anubis tries to kill him. The motif also appears in Greek myth (Phaedra and Hippolytus; Bellerophon in the Iliad, book 6). Verdict: the motif of the rejected woman's false charge was widespread, so a direct borrowing cannot be shown. What the parallel does show is that Genesis tells the story in a form Egyptians would have recognized. The rest of the two tales is very different: Bata's story turns into a myth of magic and rebirth.

a: locked him in the prison house
p: An accused slave would normally be killed. Joseph is only imprisoned.
b: Under ancient law a slave accused of assaulting his master's wife could expect death. Potiphar's "anger flared," but he put Joseph in the royal prison, the place for the king's prisoners. Some commentators (and the Midrash) think Potiphar did not fully believe his wife. The text does not say whose anger burned, Potiphar's against Joseph or against his wife. Psalm 105:17–19 remembers this time: "They tormented his foot with fetters; / his neck went into iron, / until the time his word came to pass." The Hebrew for "prison" here, beit hassohar, "the round house," appears only in the Joseph story.

a: He showed him loyal love
p: God shows Joseph hesed, covenant love, at his lowest point.
b: Hesed is the Bible's word for loyal, generous, committed love, especially within a covenant. The chapter's frame repeats "the LORD was with Joseph" at the start (39:2–3) and here at the end (39:21–23): the same presence that made him prosper in a good house is still with him in prison.

a: the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and the baker
p: Both were trusted palace officials, responsible for what went into the king's mouth.
b: The "cupbearer" (mashqeh, literally "one who gives drink") served the king's wine and was often a close confidant; Nehemiah held this post under the Persian king (Nehemiah 1:11–2:1). Egyptian palace records name many royal butlers, some of them foreigners. The baker oversaw the king's bread. Since poisoning was a real danger at royal courts, an offense by either could be serious. The text does not say what they did.

a: Don't interpretations belong to God?
p: Joseph insists that the meaning of dreams comes from God, as Daniel will at Babylon.
b: Egypt had professional dream readers with written manuals (see 41:8). Joseph claims no technique; he says the meaning belongs to God, and then offers to listen. He says it again to Pharaoh (41:16). Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar the same: "there is a God in heaven who uncovers secrets" (Daniel 2:27–28). Joseph and Daniel are the Bible's two great interpreters of a foreign king's dreams, and the book of Daniel seems to draw on Joseph's story (see the note at 41:38).

a: Pharaoh will lift up your head
t: "Lift up your head": a triple play
p: Joseph uses the same idiom for both men, with opposite meanings.
b: To "lift up someone's head" meant to restore or honor him (2 Kings 25:27, where the Babylonian king releases Jehoiachin from prison; Psalm 3:3). It may also echo the language of a census or roll call, "lifting the head" of each person counted (Numbers 1:2), as the king reviews his servants at his birthday feast (40:20). For the baker, Joseph adds a grim twist: Pharaoh will lift up your head "off of you" (40:19). The narrator uses the phrase for both men in 40:20, leaving the reader to hear both meanings.

a: keep me in mind when things are going well for you
p: The rabbis said Joseph stayed in prison two more years for trusting a man instead of God.
b: Joseph's plea is natural, and his words "do me a kindness" use the word hesed, loyal kindness. The Midrash (Genesis Rabbah 89) and Rashi on 40:23 say that because Joseph relied on the cupbearer, saying "remember me" and "mention me," he had to wait two more years (41:1), one for each request. They link it with Psalm 40:4, "Happy is the man who has set his trust on the LORD." Most modern readers do not blame Joseph; the narrator presents the delay simply as human forgetfulness that God's timing overrules.

a: I was stolen away, stolen from the land of the Hebrews
p: Joseph says he was "stolen" and does not mention his brothers. Kidnapping was a capital crime in Israel's law.
b: The Hebrew doubles the verb: gunnov gunnavti, "I was surely stolen." Exodus 21:16 and Deuteronomy 24:7 make kidnapping a person to sell him a crime punished by death. Joseph tells the truth but leaves out who stole him. "The land of the Hebrews" is an odd phrase, since Canaan was not yet Israel's land; it may reflect how Egyptians named the region, or the way later readers thought of it. He also calls his prison "this pit" (bor), the same word as the dry cistern of 37:24.

a: He will hang you on a tree
p: Probably the body was displayed on a pole after execution, and left unburied for the birds.
b: Since Pharaoh first "lifts the head off," the hanging probably means displaying the corpse on a pole or stake. To an Egyptian, being left for the birds meant losing the burial that the afterlife depended on, a fate worse than death. Israel's law later required that a body hung on a tree be buried the same day (Deuteronomy 21:22–23), a text Paul applies to the crucifixion of Jesus (Galatians 3:13). Compare the impalings in Esther 7:10 and Joshua 8:29.

a: which was Pharaoh's birthday
p: The only birthday celebration in the Old Testament is a pharaoh's.
b: Royal birthdays were celebrated in Egypt, most clearly in Ptolemaic times (the Rosetta Stone, 196 BC, decrees a festival for the king's birthday); earlier evidence is less clear. In the New Testament, Herod's birthday banquet is the occasion of John the Baptist's execution (Mark 6:21–28). Some scholars link the royal birthday with a coronation day, when kings often granted pardons.

a: He forgot all about him
p: The chapter ends in silence: two more years pass before anyone remembers Joseph.
b: The doubled statement, "gave no thought to Joseph... forgot all about him," makes the cupbearer's failure complete. Ecclesiastes 9:15–16 tells of a poor wise man who saved a city, "But not a soul remembered that poor man." The irony is that God is the one who "remembers" in Genesis (8:1, Noah; 19:29, Abraham; 30:22, Rachel), and Joseph's rescue will come from that remembering, not from a courtier. Joseph later names his firstborn Manasseh, "for God has made me forget all my hardship" (41:51).

a: standing by the Nile
p: The Hebrew says ye'or, an Egyptian word for the Nile. Egypt's whole life depended on it.
b: Ye'or comes from Egyptian itrw, "river," and in the Bible it almost always means the Nile. Egypt gets almost no rain; its harvest depended on the yearly flood of the Nile. A low flood meant famine. That is why Pharaoh's cows come up out of the river: the river decides whether Egypt eats. The word for "reeds" in 41:2, 'achu, is also an Egyptian loanword, for marsh grass.

a: seven cows, fine-looking and fat
p: Cattle and grain were Egypt's wealth. Seven stands for a full cycle.
b: Cattle grazing in the Nile marshes and grain on the riverbanks were the two pillars of Egypt's economy. Hathor, a major goddess of the Nile and fertility, was often shown as a cow. Seven, the number of the days of creation, marks a complete period. The image of lean devouring fat, and thin grain swallowing full, tells the meaning before Joseph explains it: famine will eat up all the plenty (41:30–31).

a: burned by the east wind
p: In Canaan, the hot dry east wind (the sirocco) blasts crops. Egypt's dry wind comes from the south.
b: The qadim, the east wind, is the scorching desert wind of Canaan that withers plants in a day (Ezekiel 17:10; Hosea 13:15; Jonah 4:8). In Egypt the hot winds (the khamsin) blow mostly from the south or southeast. Critics take the "east wind" as a sign that the story was told by people who lived in Canaan; others answer that qadim had simply become the standard Hebrew word for a scorching wind, whatever its direction. Either way, the picture is of grain dried out before it can fill.

a: all the magicians of Egypt
p: The Hebrew word comes from Egyptian, the title of a learned priest who read sacred texts.
b: Chartummim is borrowed from the Egyptian title chery-tep, short for "chief lector priest," the priest who read ritual texts and was famed for magic and learning. The same word is used for Pharaoh's magicians in the exodus story (Exodus 7:11) and for Babylon's experts in Daniel (Daniel 1:20; 2:2). Egypt had written dream manuals: the Chester Beatty Dream Book (Papyrus Chester Beatty III, about 1200s BC) lists dreams and their meanings, such as "If a man sees himself in a dream... good; it means..." Pharaoh's experts had the books but not the answer.

a: Today I must bring my failings to mind
p: The cupbearer's word is "sins": he admits his old offense and his forgetting.
b: The Hebrew is literally "my sins I am remembering today." He may mean the offense that put him in prison (40:1, the same verb "did wrong") or his failure to remember Joseph, or both. Either way, the man who "forgot" (40:23) now "remembers," and the two-year silence ends.

a: He shaved, changed his clothes
p: Egyptian men were clean-shaven. Joseph is made to look like an Egyptian before the king.
b: Egyptian art shows Egyptian men without beards and with shaved or closely cropped heads, while Semites from Canaan are drawn with full beards and long hair. A famous painting in the tomb of Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan (about 1890 BC) shows a group of bearded Asiatics in brightly patterned clothes arriving in Egypt. For an Israelite, shaving could be a sign of shame or mourning (2 Samuel 10:4; Isaiah 15:2); for an Egyptian court it was simply proper. Joseph's change of clothes is the third in his story (see the note at 39:12).

a: It is not in me
p: Joseph's first word to Pharaoh is a single Hebrew word: bil'adai, "apart from me."
b: Bil'adai means "without me" or "not I." Before the most powerful man in the world, Joseph disclaims any power of his own, as he did in prison (40:8). The phrase "an answer for his good" (literally "God will answer the peace [shalom] of Pharaoh") shows Joseph's confidence that the answer will help the king.

a: Pharaoh's dreams are one and the same
p: Joseph explains why the dream came twice: God has firmly decided and will act soon.
b: Joseph's own two dreams (37:5–9), the prisoners' two dreams (40:5), and now Pharaoh's two dreams follow the rule he states in 41:32: when a dream is doubled, "God has settled the matter." Doubling for certainty is common in biblical speech ("Amen, amen"; Isaiah's "comfort, comfort" in Isaiah 40:1). Joseph names God four times in his answer (41:25, 28, 32 twice), to a king who was himself thought to be divine.

a: But after them seven years of famine will come
p: Ancient texts from Egypt, Mesopotamia and Ugarit speak of seven-year famines.
b: An inscription carved on a rock on Sehel Island near Aswan in Ptolemaic times (about 200 BC), the "Famine Stela," describes seven years of low Nile floods in the reign of King Djoser (about 2600 BC) and how a god ended them. In the Gilgamesh Epic the god Anu warns of seven years of empty harvests (tablet VI), and in the Ugaritic poem of Aqhat a drought lasts seven years. Egyptian records also show real periods of failed floods, for example around 2200–2100 BC. Verdict: the seven-year famine was a known pattern, so these parallels show the story's world rather than a source.

a: take a fifth of the harvest
p: Joseph proposes storing a fifth of the harvest. A fifth later becomes a permanent tax (47:24).
b: Taxing harvests and storing grain in state granaries was standard practice in Egypt; tomb models and paintings show scribes recording grain as it is poured into silos. A fifth in good years was a heavy but realistic levy. The verb for "take a fifth" (chimmesh) appears only here. In 47:24–26 the fifth becomes a permanent rent paid to Pharaoh by farmers who have sold him their land.

a: a man who has the spirit of God in him
p: A foreign king sees "the spirit of God" in a Hebrew captive. Daniel's story follows the same pattern.
b: Pharaoh's words return almost exactly in Daniel, where a Babylonian king and queen say Daniel has "the spirit of the holy gods" in him (Daniel 4:8–9; 5:11–14). The parallels are many: a young Hebrew exile, a king's dream, failed experts, God as the source of the meaning, promotion to high office, a new foreign name (41:45; Daniel 1:7) and a gold chain (41:42; Daniel 5:29). Most scholars think Daniel's author shaped his stories with Joseph in mind. Bezalel is also filled with "the spirit of God" for wisdom and skill (Exodus 31:3).
r: Daniel 4:8–9; Daniel 5:11–14; Daniel 5:29; Daniel 1:7; Exodus 31:3; Numbers 27:18

a: all my people will obey your every word
t: "On your mouth all my people will kiss"
p: The Hebrew is a puzzle. It says literally "on your mouth all my people will kiss."
b: Al-pikha yishshaq kol-'ammi most likely means that all the people will submit to Joseph's commands, perhaps by kissing as a sign of homage (compare Psalm 2:12; 1 Samuel 10:1). Targum Onkelos and Rashi take the verb from a related root meaning "to be provided for": "by your word all my people will be fed." Others connect it to a root meaning "to arm" or "to order." All agree on the point: Joseph's word will be law.

a: the signet ring
p: Each gift matches Egyptian custom: a seal of authority, royal linen, and the "gold of honor."
b: The signet ring let Joseph seal documents in Pharaoh's name, like Mordecai with the Persian king's ring (Esther 8:2). The "fine linen" (shesh, an Egyptian loanword) was the dress of priests and nobles. Egyptian tomb scenes of the New Kingdom show the king rewarding officials by hanging gold collars around their necks, the "gold of honor." Kitchen and Hoffmeier stress how well these details fit Egyptian practice; Redford answers that such customs lasted for many centuries and do not fix a date.

a: Abrek!
p: No one knows for certain what the herald's cry means. The guesses are many.
b: Avrekh appears only here. Suggestions: Hebrew "Kneel!" (from berekh, "knee"), the reading behind the KJV's "Bow the knee"; Egyptian ib r.k, "Attention!" or "Make way!"; or Akkadian abarakku, a title for a high steward. The rabbis played on the sound: Rashi quotes the Sifre, where Rabbi Judah reads it as av rakh, "father in wisdom, tender in years," and another sage objects that it simply means "knees." The Plain English keeps the word untranslated.

a: Zaphenath-paneah
p: Probably Egyptian for "God speaks and he lives." Jewish tradition read it as "revealer of secrets."
b: Most Egyptologists, following Georg Steindorff, take Tsafenat Pa'neach as Egyptian Djed-pa-netjer-iw.f-ankh, "the god speaks and he lives." Kenneth Kitchen proposed instead "(Joseph) who is called Ip-ankh," a common Middle Kingdom name. Donald Redford answered that this name type, like Asenath, "belonging to Neith," becomes common only in the Third Intermediate and Saite periods (about 1070–525 BC), when the goddess Neith of Sais was most honored, and so points to a late date for the story. Josephus gives the meaning "revealer of secrets" (Antiquities 2.91), and Targum Onkelos and Rashi explain it from Hebrew: tsafan, "hidden," plus pa'neach, "revealer," so "revealer of hidden things." Like Daniel (Daniel 1:7), Joseph receives a court name that makes him an insider in a foreign kingdom.

a: Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On
p: Joseph marries into the priestly family of Egypt's great sun-temple city.
b: On is Heliopolis, "Sun City," near modern Cairo, the center of the worship of the sun god Ra (Jeremiah 43:13 calls it Beth-shemesh, "house of the sun"). Potiphera means "the one whom Ra gave," the same name as Potiphar (37:36). Asenath probably means "belonging to [the goddess] Neith." This marriage troubled later Jewish readers. The Greek romance Joseph and Aseneth (written roughly 100 BC to AD 200) tells of Aseneth's conversion to Joseph's God. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and the Midrash make her Dinah's daughter, raised in Potiphera's house.

a: Joseph was thirty
p: Thirteen years have passed since he was sold. Thirty is also David's age at his crowning.
b: Joseph was seventeen in 37:2, so he spent thirteen years as a slave and prisoner. Thirty was a recognized age of maturity for public service: priests began their service at thirty (Numbers 4:3), David became king at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4), and Jesus was "about thirty" when he began his ministry (Luke 3:23). Christian writers often noted the match with Jesus as part of Joseph's typology.

a: for God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's house
p: The two names are puns: "Making me forget" and "Double fruitful."
b: Manasseh, Menashsheh, sounds like nashshani, "he made me forget." Ephraim (41:52) sounds like hifrani, "he made me fruitful," echoing the blessing "be fruitful" (1:28; 35:11). The first name is surprising: Joseph thanks God for making him forget his father's house. Some read this as Joseph settling into Egypt and putting the past behind him; others note that the story will soon force him to remember (42:9). "The land of my suffering" shows that even in high office, Egypt is still the place of his affliction.
orig: מְנַשֶּׁה... נַשַּׁנִי (Menashsheh... nashshani); אֶפְרָיִם... הִפְרַנִי (Efrayim... hifrani)

a: Do whatever he tells you
p: Pharaoh's words to the hungry crowd return in Mary's words at the wedding at Cana.
b: In the Septuagint, Pharaoh says ho ean eipē hymin poiēsate. In John 2:5 Mary tells the servants at Cana, ho ti an legē hymin poiēsate, "Do whatever he tells you," before Jesus turns water into wine. Many commentators hear a deliberate echo, with Jesus as the new Joseph who provides for those in need. The same words also recall Israel's pledge at Sinai, "Whatever the LORD has said, we will do!" (Exodus 19:8).

a: the whole world came to Egypt to buy grain
p: The whole earth depends on Joseph, and so does Jacob's family, which sets up the next chapter.
b: "The whole earth" is a common Hebrew way of saying "everyone around," but it also fulfills the pattern of 12:3: through Abraham's family the nations are kept alive. Psalm 105:16–22 retells this: God "called down famine on the land... he sent a man before them, Joseph." Jesus' saying "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35) has often been read alongside Joseph's role as the one who gives the world bread.

a: Jacob kept at home and did not send with the others
p: Jacob still plays favorites. Benjamin, Rachel's other son, has taken Joseph's place.
b: Jacob calls Benjamin "Joseph's brother," as if the others were not. In 42:38 he says "he is the only one left," meaning the only son of Rachel left, in front of ten other sons. The favoritism that started the trouble (37:3) has not changed. The rest of the story tests whether the brothers will treat Benjamin the way they treated Joseph. Judah's speech in 44:18–34 quotes Jacob's painful words and shows that the brothers have learned to accept them.

a: bowed low before him, faces to the earth
p: The brothers bow to the ground, as Joseph's dream of the sheaves foretold.
b: In the dream the brothers' sheaves bowed to Joseph's (37:7). Now they come for grain and bow "faces to the earth." They will bow again in 43:26, 43:28, 44:14 and 50:18. Joseph alone notices (42:9). The irony is sharp: their effort to stop the dream ("we will see what becomes of his dreams," 37:20) has made it happen.

a: he acted like a stranger to them
p: Two forms of one Hebrew root: Joseph "recognized" them and "made himself a stranger" to them.
b: Vayyakkirem vayyitnakker: the same root nakar gives "recognize" and, in another form, "make oneself unknown, act as a foreigner." The story turns on recognition: Jacob recognized the bloody robe (37:33), Judah recognized his seal and staff (38:26), and now the brothers fail to recognize Joseph. He was seventeen when they last saw him; now he is a shaved, linen-clad Egyptian lord about 38 years old who speaks through an interpreter (42:23).

a: You are spies
p: Is Joseph taking revenge, testing his brothers, or working out his own pain? Readers disagree.
b: Joseph accuses, imprisons and frightens his brothers for two chapters. A test: most traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, see a plan to find out whether the brothers have changed, especially toward Benjamin; Ramban argued that Joseph was also arranging for the dreams to be fulfilled, which required Benjamin and finally Jacob to come. Mixed motives: many modern readers (Alter, Westermann) see real anger and hurt alongside the testing; Joseph weeps three times (42:24; 43:30; 45:2). Discipline: some Christian writers compare it to the way God brings people to confess their sin before revealing his mercy.

a: where the land lies exposed
p: Egypt guarded its eastern border with forts, so spies from Canaan were a real concern.
b: The Hebrew is literally "the nakedness of the land," its weak and exposed places. Egypt's border with Sinai was guarded: the Middle Kingdom Prophecy of Neferti speaks of the "Walls of the Ruler" built to keep Asiatics out, and the Tale of Sinuhe describes a fugitive slipping past the border forts at night. Ten armed men from Canaan arriving together could look like a scouting party.

a: as Pharaoh lives
p: Joseph swears the way an Egyptian official would.
b: Israelites swore "as the LORD lives" (Judges 8:19; 1 Samuel 14:39). Egyptian documents use oaths by the life of the king, who was held to be a god's son. Joseph's oath, said twice (42:15, 16), helps him play his part as an Egyptian lord and keeps the brothers from suspecting a fellow Hebrew. Rashi (on 42:16) adds a sharper point: whenever Joseph meant to swear falsely, he swore by the life of Pharaoh.

a: for I am a man who fears God
p: A hint, which the brothers miss: the Egyptian lord says he lives in the fear of God.
b: To "fear God" in Genesis means to have a conscience that respects God's moral order even toward strangers. Abraham once lied because he thought "There is no fear of God at all in this place" (20:11), and God said of Abraham, "now I know that you fear God" (22:12). The midwives in Egypt "feared God" and refused Pharaoh's order (Exodus 1:17). Joseph's words should reassure the brothers that he will not treat them unjustly, and they hint at who he really is.

a: We watched his anguish as he begged us for mercy
p: We learn only now that Joseph pleaded from the pit. Twenty years later the brothers still hear it.
b: Chapter 37 never told us that Joseph cried out. The narrator saves it for the brothers' own confession, so we hear it through their guilt. Their words link punishment to sin: "distress" (tsarah) for "distress." It is the first sign that they have changed, and Joseph's tears in 42:24 show what it means to him. Reuben's "I told you so" (42:22) uses the language of blood being "required," as God requires blood in 9:5.

a: through an interpreter
p: Joseph spoke Hebrew (or a related language) but used an Egyptian interpreter to keep up his disguise.
b: Egyptian officials who dealt with foreigners used interpreters; the Amarna letters (1300s BC) show that diplomatic contact with Canaan was carried on in Akkadian through scribes. The Hebrew word melits elsewhere means a go-between or spokesman (Job 33:23; 2 Chronicles 32:31). The note explains how the brothers could speak freely about their guilt in front of Joseph, not knowing he understood every word.

a: he took Simeon from among them
p: The text gives no reason. The rabbis said Simeon had led the attack on Joseph.
b: Reuben was the oldest, but he had tried to save Joseph (42:22), so Joseph passed him over. Rashi, following the Midrash (Genesis Rabbah), says Simeon was the one who threw Joseph into the pit and who first said "Here comes that master dreamer" (37:19); Joseph also wanted to separate Simeon from Levi, his partner in violence at Shechem (34:25; 49:5–7). Taking the second-oldest also let Joseph test whether the brothers would come back for one of Leah's sons.

a: What is this God has done to us?
p: The brothers see God's hand in the returned silver. They are right, though not the way they think.
b: This is the brothers' first mention of God in the story. They fear that God is punishing them, and they are partly right: God is working through Joseph to bring them to account. Joseph returned the silver as a test or a kindness; the steward will later call it a gift from "your God" (43:23). The story never shows God acting directly, but the characters keep naming him, and Joseph will finally interpret it all (45:5–8; 50:20).

a: You are making me childless!
p: Jacob's grief puts himself first: "Me you have made childless... it all falls on me."
b: The Hebrew puts "me" first for emphasis: oti shikkaltem, "it is me you have bereaved." The verb shakal, to lose children, returns in Jacob's resigned words in 43:14, "if I am bereaved, I am bereaved." He suspects his sons ("you"), possibly guessing more about Joseph than he says. The last words, "all these are upon me," mean that every loss lands on him.

a: Put my two sons to death if I do not bring him to you
p: Reuben offers his own sons' lives. Jacob ignores him.
b: Reuben means well but offers something useless and terrible: losing two grandsons would not comfort Jacob for losing a son. Rashi quotes the Midrash (Genesis Rabbah 91), where Jacob calls him "a foolish firstborn: are your sons not my sons?" Jacob does not even answer him. Compare Judah's offer in 43:9, which puts Judah himself on the line and which Jacob accepts. The contrast prepares for 49:3–4 and 49:8–12, where Judah, not Reuben, receives the leading blessing.

a: The man gave us a stern warning
p: From here on Judah, not Reuben, speaks for the brothers.
b: In chapter 37 Reuben and Judah both made proposals; in chapter 42 Reuben spoke (42:22, 37). Now Judah takes charge: he reasons with his father (43:3–5), pledges himself for Benjamin (43:8–10), leads the brothers back to Joseph (44:14), speaks for them all (44:16), and makes the great plea of 44:18–34. Jacob sends him ahead in 46:28. Genesis is tracing how the son who sold his brother becomes the leader of the family, which explains his blessing in 49:8–12.

a: I will be his guarantor
p: Judah becomes Benjamin's surety, taking on himself the blame if the boy is lost.
b: The verb 'arav means to stand as surety, to guarantee another person's debt with one's own life or property (Proverbs 6:1; 11:15). It is related to 'eravon, the "pledge" that Tamar took from Judah (38:17–18). The man who once gave a pledge for pleasure now gives himself as a pledge for his brother, and in 44:32–33 he makes good on it. Hebrews 7:22 calls Jesus the "guarantee" (Greek engyos) of a better covenant; Christian readers have long seen Judah's pledge as a picture of that.

a: a little balm, a little honey, gum and myrrh, pistachios and almonds
t: The same goods, going the other way
p: Jacob sends the very products that the caravan carried when it took Joseph to Egypt.
b: Balm, gum and myrrh (ladanum) were the cargo of the Ishmaelites who bought Joseph (37:25). Now Jacob, unknowing, sends them as a gift to the son whose sale they paid for. "Honey" (devash) here probably means a thick syrup of dates or grapes, a delicacy in the hill country. Pistachios (botnim) are mentioned only here in the Bible. Jacob's gift recalls his approach to Esau with a present to win his favor (32:13–20).

a: May God Almighty
p: Jacob uses the name with which God gave the family its promises of many children.
b: El Shaddai (traditionally "God Almighty") is the name God used with Abraham and Jacob when promising offspring and blessing (17:1; 28:3; 35:11; compare Exodus 6:3). Its meaning is uncertain: "God of the mountain," "God who is sufficient" (the rabbinic she-dai), or a name linked with shadayim, "breasts," which 49:25 seems to play on. Jacob, about to lose another son, appeals to the God of the promise of many sons.

a: if I am bereaved, I am bereaved
p: Jacob's resigned words sound like Esther's before she risks her life.
b: The repeated verb expresses acceptance of what cannot be changed. Esther uses the same pattern before going unsummoned to the Persian king: "If I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:16). Esther's story, set in a foreign court with a Jewish official rising to power, has many echoes of Joseph's. Jacob's surrender of Benjamin is the turning point that makes the reunion possible.

a: He means to roll over us, fall on us, and take us for slaves
p: The brothers fear being made slaves, the very thing they did to Joseph.
b: The verbs are vivid: literally "to roll himself upon us and fall upon us." Their fear of being seized as slaves mirrors their own crime. They confess at once to the steward before anyone accuses them (43:20–22). Many commentators see in this the working of conscience: Proverbs 28:1 says "the wicked flee with no one after them." Readers who see Joseph's actions as discipline point to scenes like this as its purpose.

a: Your God, the God of your father, put treasure in your sacks
p: An Egyptian steward speaks of "your God, the God of your father." Who taught him to say that?
b: The steward knows more than the brothers do. He may simply be following Joseph's instructions, or he may have learned something of Joseph's faith. His words echo Jacob's own name for God (31:42, 53). He says "peace to you" (shalom lakhem), the words the brothers could not speak to Joseph (37:4). Many readers see in him an outsider who has learned from Joseph to see God's hand in events.

a: his heart burned with love for his brother
p: The Hebrew word for compassion comes from the word for womb: Joseph is overcome with love for his mother's son.
b: Nikhmeru rachamav, "his compassions grew hot." Rachamim, compassion, is the plural of rechem, womb, the deep love one feels for family. The same phrase describes the true mother in Solomon's judgment (1 Kings 3:26) and God's love for Ephraim (Hosea 11:8). This is the second time Joseph weeps (42:24; 45:2, 14–15; 46:29; 50:1, 17). Benjamin is the only brother born of his mother Rachel.

a: because Egyptians could not share a meal with Hebrews
p: Egyptians would not share a table with foreigners. The Greek historian Herodotus reports the same.
b: Herodotus says that Egyptians would not kiss a Greek or use a Greek's knife or cooking pot, because Greeks ate cows, which were sacred to Isis (Histories 2.41). Whether that custom goes back to Joseph's time is unknown. The word "detestable" (to'evah) is used again of Egyptian contempt for shepherds (46:34) and for Israelite sacrifices (Exodus 8:26). Joseph eats alone because, as an Egyptian lord, he could not eat with Hebrews, and as a Hebrew he may not have been welcome at the Egyptians' table either.

a: the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth
p: Joseph seats his brothers from oldest to youngest. The brothers are amazed: how could an Egyptian know?
b: There were eleven brothers, with four mothers, and some close in age; the odds of guessing their order by chance are tiny. The brothers look at each other in alarm, and the scene adds to their sense that something uncanny is going on. Joseph's cup is later said to be used for divining (44:5), and Rashi pictures Joseph tapping the cup and "reading" their order. Literary readers note that this ordered seating reverses chapter 37's chaos.

a: Benjamin's was five times as large as anyone else's
p: Joseph favors Benjamin openly. Will his brothers resent him, as they resented Joseph?
b: Favoritism caused the hatred of chapter 37: a father's love and a special robe. Now an Egyptian lord heaps five times as much food on Rachel's younger son. If the brothers are still the same, they will be jealous. Instead, the text says simply that they "drank deep" with him. The test will be repeated more severely with the silver cup (44:2) and, after the reunion, with Benjamin's five changes of clothes (45:22).

a: put my cup, the silver cup, in the mouth of the youngest one's sack
p: Joseph sets up Benjamin to be enslaved. Will the brothers abandon Rachel's other son?
b: The plan recreates the situation of chapter 37 as exactly as possible. Rachel's son, the father's favorite, will be lost to slavery in Egypt, and this time the brothers would be blameless if they went home. They could even return with grain, silver and an excuse. Joseph wants to know whether they will save themselves or stand by Benjamin. Maimonides defined complete repentance as facing the same situation with the same ability to sin and choosing not to (Laws of Repentance 2:1); many Jewish commentators see Judah's response in exactly those terms.

a: what he reads omens with
p: Reading omens from liquid in a cup was a known practice. Did Joseph really do it?
b: The verb nachash means to practice divination, which Israel's law later forbids (Leviticus 19:26; Deuteronomy 18:10). Mesopotamian texts from the Old Babylonian period describe divining by pouring oil on water in a cup and reading the shapes (lecanomancy). Joseph has the steward say this, and later claims it himself (44:15), to make the theft look serious and his knowledge look uncanny. Many Jewish and Christian commentators (for example Ramban) hold that Joseph was only playing the part of an Egyptian lord; the story never shows him using the cup, and he has always credited God with his knowledge (40:8; 41:16).

a: Whichever of your servants has it on him must die
p: The brothers' oath recalls Jacob's oath when Rachel had secretly stolen Laban's gods.
b: When Laban accused Jacob's household of stealing his household gods, Jacob swore, "Whoever has them will not live," not knowing that Rachel had them (31:32). Now Rachel's son is the one found with the stolen object. The steward softens the terms (44:10), as if the outcome had been planned all along, which it had.

a: They tore their clothes
p: The brothers tear their clothes, as Reuben and Jacob did over Joseph.
b: In chapter 37 Reuben tore his clothes at the empty pit (37:29) and Jacob tore his at the bloody robe (37:34). Now all the brothers tear theirs for Benjamin, and all go back together, though only Benjamin was accused. That single detail answers Joseph's question: they will not leave him.

a: God has found out your servants' guilt
p: Judah confesses guilt for a theft they did not commit, but he means the crime they did.
b: Judah does not argue about the cup. He says that God has "found" their guilt, using the same verb as the finding of the cup (44:12). He seems to mean the old sin against Joseph, which no one in Egypt knows about. Most readers see here the brothers' full confession: they accept punishment as a group, "we and the one in whose hand the cup was found." This echoes Judah's own words to Tamar ("she is in the right, not I," 38:26).

a: Then Judah came close to him
p: Judah's plea is the longest speech in Genesis. A weekly Torah reading begins with its first word.
b: The synagogue cycle of Torah readings names its sections by their first words. Vayigash, "Then he came close," begins at 44:18 and runs to 47:27. Judah's speech (44:18–34) is the longest in Genesis and has been admired by readers of every kind. It is courteous, never mentions the cup, retells the story from the family's side, quotes the father's grief, and ends by offering himself. The Midrash pictures Judah ready to fight if necessary; the text itself shows only humility and love.

a: he alone is left of his mother's sons, and his father loves him
p: Judah repeats, without bitterness, the favoritism that once made the brothers hate Joseph.
b: In chapter 37 the father's love for Rachel's son led to hatred and a sale. Now Judah tells a stranger that his father loves this son, and even quotes Jacob saying "my wife bore me two sons" (44:27), as if Leah and her sons did not count. Judah does not complain. He has come to accept his father's preference and to put his father's grief before his own hurt. Many readers find this the moral center of the whole story.

a: He is torn, surely torn to pieces
p: Judah quotes Jacob's cry about Joseph, the very lie the brothers told.
b: The doubled verb tarof toraf repeats Jacob's words in 37:33. Judah, who helped sell Joseph and send the bloody robe, now has to quote his father's belief in the lie, to the brother himself. He says, "I have not seen him to this day." The reader knows that the father's lost son is standing in front of the speaker.

a: since his life is bound up with the boy's life
p: The same phrase describes Jonathan's love for David.
b: "His soul is tied to his soul": the expression returns in 1 Samuel 18:1, where "Jonathan's life was tied up with David's life," with the same Hebrew verb, qashar. It describes a bond so close that one cannot survive the loss of the other. Judah argues not from law but from love: taking Benjamin would kill their father.

a: please let your servant stay as my lord's slave in place of the boy
p: Judah offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place. Jews and Christians both see the climax of the story here.
b: The one who proposed selling Joseph as a slave (37:27) now offers to become a slave so that Rachel's other son can go free. Jewish readers see the model of teshuvah, repentance shown by action, and the reason the kingship went to Judah (49:8–10; the Midrash and the Tosefta connect Judah's leadership with his confessions). Christian readers have often seen a picture of substitution: Jesus, from the tribe of Judah, takes the place of the guilty (Hebrews 7:14; Mark 10:45). Both see a brother willing to pay with his own freedom.

a: Joseph could no longer hold himself back
p: The verb is the same one used when Joseph forced back his tears at dinner (43:31).
b: Hit'appeq means to control oneself, to hold back. In 43:31 Joseph "controlled himself" and ordered the meal. Now he cannot. He clears the room so that the brothers' shame is not seen by Egyptians, and so that the moment belongs to the family alone. Rashi notes he would not let them be embarrassed before strangers.

a: I am Joseph
p: Two Hebrew words, ani Yosef. His first question is about his father.
b: Joseph has already been told that Jacob is alive (43:27–28), so his question is less a request for information than a cry from the heart: Is my father, the man you have been describing, really still alive? Some readers also hear a rebuke: did you think of my father when you sold me? The brothers are "terrified" (nivhalu), a strong word for panic before power. The scene has been read by Christians as a picture of Jesus revealing himself to his own (Luke 24:36–39; John 20:19–20), and by Jews as a picture of reconciliation that comes after repentance.

a: God sent me here before you to keep people alive
p: Three times Joseph says God sent him (45:5, 7, 8). This is the theological heart of the story.
b: Joseph does not say the brothers did nothing wrong; he says "you sold me" (45:4). But he places their act inside God's larger purpose: "to keep people alive" (literally "for the preserving of life"). He returns to this in 50:20. Readers have drawn different lessons. Many Christians see a clear statement of providence: God's purpose works through human evil without excusing it (Acts 2:23; Romans 8:28). Jewish tradition sees God fulfilling his word to Abraham that his descendants would go down to a foreign land (15:13). Some modern readers ask whether Joseph's framing lets the brothers off too easily; the story itself returns to their guilt in 50:15–17.

a: to keep a remnant alive for you on the earth
p: Joseph uses two words that the prophets later use for God's rescue of Israel.
b: She'erit, "remnant," means the survivors who are left after a disaster; peletah, "escape, deliverance," means a group that gets away. Both words later become key terms in the prophets for the faithful who survive judgment (Isaiah 10:20–22; Joel 2:32; Micah 4:7), and Paul speaks of a "remnant chosen by grace" (Romans 11:5). Here they describe a family saved from famine.

a: He has made me a father to Pharaoh
p: This sounds like an Egyptian court title: "God's father," given to senior advisers and priests.
b: Egyptian officials could bear the title it-netjer, "god's father," an honorific for priests and for senior counselors of the king (who was himself regarded as a god's son). Joseph's three titles, father to Pharaoh, lord of his household, ruler of all Egypt, sum up his rise. Isaiah 22:21 calls a royal steward a "father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem."

a: the land of Goshen
p: Good grazing land in the eastern Nile Delta, near the route to Canaan.
b: Goshen has not been located exactly, but most scholars place it in the eastern Delta, around the Wadi Tumilat, a valley leading east toward Sinai. The Septuagint calls it "Gesem of Arabia." Egyptian texts describe officials letting herders from Sinai and Canaan water their flocks in this region in dry years, for example a border report from about 1200 BC (Papyrus Anastasi VI) about letting Edomite shepherds through to the pools of Pithom. Israel lives in Goshen until the exodus (Exodus 8:22; 9:26).

a: After that his brothers talked with him
p: Once they "could not speak to him in peace" (37:4). Now they talk with him.
b: The story began with hatred so strong that the brothers "could not speak to him in peace" (37:4). The reconciliation ends with "his brothers spoke with him," the same verb, now with no barrier. The narrator does not tell us what they said. The weeping and kissing on the neck recall Esau and Jacob's reunion (33:4) and Jacob and Joseph's (46:29).

a: to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothes
p: Joseph gives Benjamin more than the others. Did he not learn from his own robe?
b: Clothes once marked Joseph as the favorite and caused the hatred (37:3). The Talmud (Megillah 16a–b) asks how Joseph could repeat his father's mistake, and answers that he was hinting at Benjamin's descendant Mordecai, who would go out "in royal clothing" before the Persian king (Esther 8:15), five garments in all. Most readers today see a final test of the brothers' jealousy, or simply Joseph's love for his only full brother, which the brothers now accept.

a: Don't get stirred up on the way
t: Don't quarrel, or don't be afraid?
p: The verb ragaz means to be agitated. Joseph may mean "don't quarrel" or "don't be anxious."
b: Al-tirgezu can mean "do not tremble, be afraid," as the peoples "shake" in Exodus 15:14. It can also mean "do not be stirred up" in anger (Proverbs 29:9). Rashi takes it as "don't argue on the way" about whose fault the sale was. Others think Joseph is reassuring them: they need not fear further tests or robbers. The Talmud (Ta'anit 10b) adds a practical reading: "don't take big steps," that is, don't rush. The Plain English keeps a phrase that allows both main senses.

a: Jacob's heart went numb, because he did not believe them
p: Jacob's heart "went cold" or "stopped"; he could not take in the news.
b: Vayyafag libbo: the verb means to grow numb, faint or cold (Psalm 77:2; Habakkuk 1:4). Jacob had believed the bloody robe without question (37:33); now he cannot believe the truth. Only when he sees the carts does "the spirit of Jacob" revive (45:27). Targum Onkelos says that "the spirit of prophecy" rested on Jacob again.

a: Israel said, "Enough! My son Joseph is still alive.
p: The narrator calls him Jacob while he is numb, Israel when he revives.
b: Through these chapters the father's two names shift. He is "Jacob" in his grief and doubt (45:25–27) and "Israel" when he acts in faith (45:28; 46:1). Many readers, from the Midrash to modern literary critics, think the change is meaningful, though the pattern is not perfectly consistent. "Israel" was the name given when he wrestled with God (32:28).

a: He came to Beersheba, and there he offered sacrifices to the God of Isaac his father
p: Jacob stops at the southern edge of Canaan to worship before leaving the promised land.
b: Beersheba was where God appeared to Isaac and Isaac built an altar (26:23–25). Isaac had been told not to go down to Egypt during a famine (26:2), and Abraham's trip to Egypt had gone badly (12:10–20). Jacob may well be asking whether he is allowed to leave. God had also told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers and slaves in a land not their own for four hundred years (15:13). Jacob's sacrifice to "the God of Isaac his father" seeks that same God's permission.

a: Jacob, Jacob
p: This is the last time God speaks directly in Genesis. The double call marks a turning point.
b: God calls a name twice at great moments: "Abraham, Abraham" at the binding of Isaac (22:11), "Moses, Moses" at the burning bush (Exodus 3:4), "Samuel, Samuel" (1 Samuel 3:10), and "Saul, Saul" on the Damascus road (Acts 9:4). Jacob answers as Abraham did, "Here I am." After these words, God never speaks aloud again in Genesis; he is known through dreams already given, through providence, and through the blessings the fathers pass on.

a: I will make you a great nation there
p: The promise to Abraham will be fulfilled outside the promised land.
b: God promised Abraham, "I will make you a great nation" (12:2). Surprisingly, it will happen in Egypt. Exodus 1:7 reports the result: "the Israelites were fruitful and swarmed. They grew many and became very, very strong." Israel's harvest confession remembered it: "My father was a wandering Aramean. He went down to Egypt and lived there as a foreigner, few in number. But there he became a nation, great, strong and many" (Deuteronomy 26:5).

a: I will go down with you to Egypt
t: God goes into exile with his people
p: Jewish tradition drew from this verse that God's presence goes with Israel into every exile.
b: God promises his own presence in Egypt and a return "surely up," a doubled verb pointing to the exodus and to Jacob's burial in Canaan (50:13). The Talmud (Megillah 29a) teaches that "wherever Israel went into exile, the Shekhinah [God's presence] went with them: to Egypt, to Babylon..." and that it will return with them. Christians have often heard a similar note in "I myself am with you every day" (Matthew 28:20). The phrase "Joseph will lay his hand on your eyes" means Joseph will be present to close his father's eyes at death.

a: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt
p: Exodus opens with the very same words, picking up the story where Genesis leaves it.
b: Exodus 1:1 begins ve'elleh shemot benei Yisra'el habba'im Mitsraymah, "These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt," exactly as here. The book of Exodus takes its Hebrew name, Shemot ("Names"), from this phrase. The two lists form a bridge between the family story of Genesis and the national story of Exodus. Numbers 26 gives a fuller list of the same clans, with some differences in spelling and order.

a: Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman
p: Only Shaul's mother is singled out. The rabbis guessed who she was.
b: Of all the mothers of Jacob's grandsons, only Shaul's is mentioned, perhaps because a Canaanite wife was notable, as with Judah (38:2). Rashi, following the Midrash, says she was Dinah, taken by Shechem the Canaanite (chapter 34), and that Simeon took her into his household. Others take it simply as a note that Simeon, like Judah, married a local woman. Numbers 26:13 lists the clan of the Shaulites without comment.

a: The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul
p: Perez was a newborn in chapter 38. Could he have two sons already? The list may be counting future clan heads.
b: If chapter 38 starts after Joseph's sale, about 22 years pass before the move to Egypt, barely enough for Judah to have grandsons through Perez. Benjamin, called "the boy" in 44:22–34, is credited with ten sons (46:21). Traditional readers answer that marriage was early, or that the timeline of chapter 38 began earlier (Ibn Ezra). Many scholars, conservative and critical, think the list counts the founding clans of Israel as later known (compare Numbers 26:20–21, 38–41), including some born in Egypt, "in the loins" of those who went down (compare Hebrews 7:9–10).

a: numbered thirty-three
t: How do the numbers add up?
p: Leah's line lists only 32 living names. Who is the thirty-third?
b: Leah's sons and grandsons, minus Er and Onan, who died in Canaan, plus Dinah, make 32. Many commentators count Jacob himself as the 33rd, since 46:8 includes him among those "who came to Egypt." Rashi, following the Talmud, counts Moses' mother Jochebed, said to have been born "between the walls" as the family entered Egypt, because Numbers 26:59 says she was "born to Levi in Egypt." The other totals do work: Zilpah's line is 16, Rachel's 14, Bilhah's 7, making 70 in all (46:27).

a: and their sister Serah
p: Only one granddaughter is named. Jewish legend made her one of the most remarkable women in the Bible.
b: Serah appears again only in Numbers 26:46 and 1 Chronicles 7:30, which means she was still remembered among the clans. The Midrash made her a living link between generations: she gently told Jacob that Joseph was alive by singing to him with a harp (Sefer HaYashar; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan), was rewarded with long life, and centuries later showed Moses where Joseph's coffin lay (Mekhilta on Exodus 13:19; Talmud Sotah 13a). Some traditions said she entered paradise alive.

a: numbered seventy
p: Seventy is a number of completeness: Israel goes down to Egypt as a complete people in miniature.
b: The family is counted as seventy, the same as the seventy nations listed in Genesis 10. Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Masoretic Text says God set the bounds of the peoples "according to the number of the sons of Israel," though a Dead Sea Scroll (4QDeut-j) reads "sons of God" and the Septuagint "angels of God," which most modern versions follow. Seventy also appears in the seventy elders of Israel (Exodus 24:1; Numbers 11:16) and in the seventy (or seventy-two) whom Jesus sends out (Luke 10:1). Exodus 1:5 and Deuteronomy 10:22 repeat the number, but the Greek Septuagint and Stephen in Acts 7:14 say seventy-five (see the variant on this verse).
r: Genesis 10; Exodus 1:5; Deuteronomy 10:22; Deuteronomy 32:8; Exodus 24:1; Luke 10:1; Acts 7:14

a: Jacob sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph
p: Judah leads the way. The rabbis said he went to set up a house of study.
