b: Judah's role as leader continues. The Hebrew verb lehorot, "to show the way," also means "to teach" (it is related to torah, "instruction"). Rashi, following the Midrash (Genesis Rabbah 95), says Judah was sent to set up a house of study in Goshen, so that the family would have a place of teaching in exile. The Septuagint reads the verse differently (see the variant).

a: fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a long while
p: The Hebrew does not make clear who wept. Rashi said Jacob did not, because he was saying the Shema.
b: The subject of "he fell on his neck and wept" is grammatically Joseph, but it could be either. Rashi, citing rabbinic tradition, says that Joseph wept but Jacob did not kiss him or weep, because at that moment he was reciting the Shema ("Hear, O Israel," Deuteronomy 6:4), directing his overwhelming joy to God. The text itself simply lets the reunion happen: twenty-two years of grief end in a long embrace.

a: I can die now
p: Like old Simeon in the temple, Jacob is ready to die in peace now that he has seen.
b: Jacob had said he would go down to Sheol mourning his son (37:35). Now he says he can die content. Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, says, "Master, now you are setting your slave free / to go in peace... with my own eyes I have seen your salvation" (Luke 2:29–30). Jacob in fact lives seventeen more years (47:28).

a: Egyptians loathe every shepherd
p: Egyptian texts look down on nomadic herders from Asia. The remark helps keep Israel separate.
b: No Egyptian text says that all shepherds were hated, and Egyptians kept large herds of their own (47:6, 17). But Egyptian writings often speak with contempt of "Asiatics," the herders of Sinai and Canaan: the Instruction for Merikare calls them "the miserable Asiatic," never settled in one place. Herodotus says that swineherds were despised (Histories 2.47). Joseph's coaching uses this prejudice to his family's advantage: Pharaoh will settle them apart, in Goshen, where they can remain a distinct people.

a: He took five of his brothers and presented them to Pharaoh
p: The text does not say. The Midrash guessed he chose the weakest-looking, so Pharaoh would not draft them.
b: Joseph chooses five out of eleven to meet Pharaoh. Rashi, following the Midrash (Genesis Rabbah 95), says he chose the least impressive so that Pharaoh would not make them soldiers. The Hebrew "from the end of his brothers" (miqtseh) can mean "some of" or "from among the whole group." Five is also a recurring number in the story: a fifth of the harvest (41:34; 47:24), Benjamin's fivefold portion (43:34) and five changes of clothes (45:22).

a: We have come to stay in the land as foreigners
p: The verb gur means to live as a resident foreigner, without rights to the land.
b: Lagur ba'arets, "to sojourn in the land." A ger was a resident alien who lived among a people without belonging to it. The brothers ask for temporary shelter, not citizenship. Israel's law later reminded them: "You know the life of a foreigner from the inside, because you were foreigners living in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 23:9). The same word lies behind Jacob's "wanderer" and "wanderings" in 47:9.

a: and Jacob blessed Pharaoh
p: The old shepherd blesses the king of Egypt, twice. Who is greater here?
b: The verb barakh can mean a formal greeting and farewell (as in 1 Samuel 13:10; 2 Kings 4:29), and Jacob does it on arriving and leaving (47:7, 10). But Genesis means more: this is the family in whom "All the clans of the earth will find blessing" (12:3), and Pharaoh, who has blessed them with land, receives blessing in return (12:3: "I will bless those who bless you"). Hebrews 7:7 states the principle that "the lesser is blessed by the greater." Rashi says Jacob blessed Pharaoh that the Nile would rise to meet him.

a: My years have been few and full of trouble
p: Jacob calls his life a sojourn: short, troubled and not his own. Later Scripture made this the model of faith.
b: Abraham lived 175 years (25:7) and Isaac 180 (35:28); Jacob will reach 147 (47:28). His summary is honest: exile from home, years with Laban, the loss of Rachel, Dinah, Joseph. Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs "admitted that they were foreigners and temporary residents on the earth"; David prays, "We are foreigners before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were" (1 Chronicles 29:15; compare Psalm 39:12; 1 Peter 2:11). A medieval Jewish tradition, less kind, says Jacob lost years of life for complaining before Pharaoh.

a: the land of Rameses
t: "The land of Rameses": an updated name?
p: The region is named after a city built for Ramesses II in the 1200s BC, long after Joseph's traditional date.
b: Pi-Ramesse, "House of Ramesses," was the Delta capital built by Ramesses II (reigned about 1279–1213 BC), near the older city of Avaris. Exodus 1:11 says Israelite slaves built "Rameses." If Joseph lived centuries earlier, the name is an anachronism. Traditional scholars explain it as a later scribe's updating of an old place name, like "Dan" in 14:14, which was named long after Abraham (Judges 18:29). Critical scholars take it as a sign that the story was told or written after the 1200s. Either way, it locates Goshen in the eastern Delta.

a: Joseph bought up all Egypt's land for Pharaoh
t: Joseph's famine policy: wise or harsh?
p: Joseph saves Egypt but makes its people Pharaoh's tenants. Readers have praised and criticized him.
b: In three steps (silver, livestock, then land and bodies), Joseph turns a free peasantry into Pharaoh's serfs paying a fifth of every harvest. Praise: the people themselves say "You have kept us alive!" (47:25); a fifth was mild by ancient standards; traditional Jewish and Christian readers saw wise stewardship. Criticism: modern readers such as Leon Kass and Aaron Wildavsky argue that Joseph built the very system of state slavery that will soon crush Israel: "a new king... who did not know Joseph" inherits it (Exodus 1:8–11). Etiology: critical scholars see a story explaining Egypt's royal ownership of land, a famous feature of Egypt known also to Greek writers (Herodotus, Histories 2.109).

a: Only the priests' land he did not buy
p: Egyptian temples owned enormous estates and enjoyed royal support.
b: Egyptian temples held vast amounts of farmland, worked by tenants and staff. Papyrus Harris I (about 1150 BC) lists huge royal gifts of land, cattle and people to the temples under Ramesses III, and the Wilbour Papyrus (about the same time) records how temple and crown land was farmed and taxed. The detail that priests received a fixed allowance from Pharaoh fits this picture. Joseph's father-in-law was himself a priest (41:45).

a: it stands to this day
p: The phrase shows that the narrator is writing long after the events, for readers who knew the custom.
b: "Until this day" (ad hayyom hazzeh) is a common formula in the Bible that links a story to something later readers could still see: a name, a pile of stones, a law (32:32; 35:20; Deuteronomy 34:6; Joshua 4:9). Traditional scholars who hold to Moses as author see such phrases either as Moses' own perspective or as later editorial notes. Critical scholars treat them as clues to the time of writing.

a: they were fruitful and multiplied greatly
p: The words of the creation blessing come true for Israel in Egypt.
b: "Be fruitful and multiply" was God's blessing on humankind (1:28; 9:1) and his promise to Jacob (35:11). Here the family takes root in Goshen and begins to grow. Exodus 1:7 repeats the words in a fuller form, "fruitful, swarmed, multiplied and became very strong," just before Pharaoh's fear turns into oppression.

a: a hundred and forty-seven years
p: The three patriarchs' life spans follow a number pattern built on squares and sevens.
b: Nahum Sarna, building on an observation by Samuel Gevirtz, points out that Abraham lived 175 years (7 × 5 × 5), Isaac 180 (5 × 6 × 6) and Jacob 147 (3 × 7 × 7). In each case the squared number rises by one (5, 6, 7) and the other factor falls by two (7, 5, 3), and in each the factors add up to 17. Many scholars think the ages were shaped to show order and design. Jacob also lived 17 years with Joseph in Canaan (37:2) and 17 with him in Egypt.

a: please put your hand under my thigh
p: The same gesture sealed Abraham's oath about a wife for Isaac.
b: Abraham had his servant place his hand under his thigh to swear he would not take a Canaanite wife for Isaac (24:2, 9). The thigh probably stands for the organs of procreation: the oath is sworn on the family line and its future. Jacob asks for hesed ve'emet, "faithful love and truth," the same pair Abraham's servant used (24:27, 49). Rashi notes that kindness to the dead is true kindness, because it cannot be repaid.

a: carry me out of Egypt and lay me in the grave where they lie
p: Jacob wants to be buried in the promised land, as a pledge that God's promise will come true.
b: Machpelah, the cave Abraham bought (23:17–20), was the family's only piece of the promised land. Being buried there was a claim on the promise. Hebrews 11:21–22 counts Jacob's blessing and Joseph's instructions about his bones as acts of faith. Jewish tradition also says Jacob did not want to be worshiped by Egyptians or to rest in impure ground (Rashi). Burial "with my fathers" also meant belonging to the family in death.

a: And Israel bowed down
p: Jacob bows, either in worship of God or to Joseph, which would fulfill the dream of 37:9–10.
b: The verb is the one used in Joseph's dream, "the sun, the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me" (37:9). Some readers think this is the father finally bowing to the son. Rashi says he bowed toward the Shekhinah, God's presence, which hovers over the head of the sick. The Talmud (Megillah 16b) quotes a proverb about the scene: "When the fox has his hour, bow down to him," meaning that even Jacob bowed to Joseph while Joseph was in power. Hebrews 11:21, following the Greek, says that Jacob "worshiped" (see the variant).

a: God Almighty appeared to me at Luz
p: Jacob recalls the promise God made to him at Luz, which he renamed Bethel.
b: Luz was the old name of Bethel, "house of God," where Jacob dreamed of the stairway to heaven (28:10–19) and where God later renewed the promise: "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and become many... kings will come out of your loins. The land I gave to Abraham and to Isaac I will give to you, and to your offspring after you" (35:11–12). Jacob quotes that promise almost word for word in 48:4. He grounds his adoption of Joseph's sons in God's word, not just his own wishes.

a: a gathering of peoples
p: The Hebrew qahal, "assembly," became in Greek synagogē and, elsewhere, ekklēsia, "church."
b: Qehal 'ammim, "an assembly of peoples," appears in the promises at 28:3 and 35:11 ("a nation and an assembly of nations"). Qahal later names Israel gathered before God (Deuteronomy 9:10; 31:30). The Septuagint translates it here with synagōgas ethnōn, and elsewhere often with ekklēsia, the word the New Testament uses for the church. Jacob's promise of many peoples within one family has been read by Christians as pointing beyond Israel's twelve tribes.

a: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine as much as Reuben and Simeon are
p: Joseph's two sons become two tribes. In effect, Joseph receives the firstborn's double share.
b: By adopting Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, Jacob gives Joseph two tribes in Israel instead of one. Under Israel's law the firstborn received a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17), and 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 explains that Reuben's birthright passed to the sons of Joseph, while leadership passed to Judah. This is why the tribal lists usually count twelve tribes even though Levi received no territory: Ephraim and Manasseh fill the gap (Numbers 1; Joshua 14:4).

a: to my sorrow Rachel died on the way
p: Jacob remembers burying Rachel by the road near Bethlehem. Jeremiah and Matthew picture her weeping there.
b: Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin and was buried "on the way to Ephrath" (35:16–20). Jacob mentions it here perhaps because Ephraim and Manasseh take the place of children Rachel never had. Rashi has Jacob apologize to Joseph for not burying her in the family tomb, and explains that God wanted her by the road so that she could weep for her children when they passed into exile. Jeremiah 31:15 hears "Rachel weeping for her children," and Matthew 2:18 applies the verse to the children of Bethlehem. A traditional Rachel's Tomb stands outside Bethlehem, though 1 Samuel 10:2 places her grave near the border of Benjamin.

a: Israel's eyes had grown heavy with age
t: Another blind father, another younger son
p: Like Isaac, Jacob is old and nearly blind when he blesses. But this time the blind man sees more clearly.
b: Isaac's eyes were "dim" when Jacob deceived him to get the blessing meant for Esau (27:1, 18–29). Now Jacob is the blind father, and he too blesses the younger son ahead of the older. The difference is that Jacob does it knowingly and on purpose (48:14, 19), while Isaac was tricked. The man who took his brother's blessing by deception now gives a younger son the first place by choice.

a: Joseph took them from between his father's knees
p: Placing a child on the knees was a gesture of adoption or acceptance into the family.
b: Rachel asked that Bilhah bear children "on my knees" so that they would count as Rachel's (30:3). Joseph's great-grandsons are "born on Joseph's knees" (50:23), and Naomi takes Obed into her lap (Ruth 4:16). Jacob has the boys at his knees as he adopts them; Joseph then takes them back and bows in thanks before presenting them for the blessing.

a: He crossed his hands
p: Jacob crosses his arms so that the right hand, the greater blessing, falls on the younger boy.
b: The verb sikkel usually means "to act wisely, deliberately"; many translators think here it means "to cross," and the KJV has "guiding his hands wittingly." The right hand was the hand of strength and honor (Psalm 110:1). Genesis keeps favoring younger sons: Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Perez, Joseph and now Ephraim, a pattern Paul uses to show that God's choice is grace, not birth order (Romans 9:10–13). Tertullian saw in the crossed arms a figure of the cross of Christ (On Baptism 8). The Plain English follows "crossed."

a: God, my shepherd from my first day until this day
p: Jacob, a shepherd all his life, is the first in the Bible to call God his shepherd.
b: Jacob tended Laban's flocks for twenty years (31:38–40). Now he calls God "the one who shepherded me." He uses the image again in 49:24. The picture runs through Scripture: "The LORD is my shepherd" (Psalm 23:1), "Shepherd of Israel" (Psalm 80:1), and Jesus' "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). Notice that the blessing is said to bless "Joseph" while it names his sons: blessing the sons is blessing the father.

a: the angel who has redeemed me from all harm
p: The first use of "redeem" in the Bible. Who is this angel?
b: Hammal'akh hago'el: the verb ga'al is the word for a family rescuer who buys back land or people (see the topic on the kinsman-redeemer). It appears here for the first time in the Bible. In the poem, the angel stands in parallel with God himself. Jacob met angels at Bethel (28:12) and Mahanaim (32:1–2) and wrestled with a "man" whom he identified with God (32:24–30; Hosea 12:3–4). Jewish tradition reads a guardian angel, and this verse became a well-known bedtime prayer for children, Hamalakh hago'el. Many church fathers saw the "angel of the LORD" as the Son of God before his birth. Critical scholars often see an older way of speaking of God's presence as a messenger.

a: his offspring will become a whole throng of nations
p: The Hebrew phrase is melo ha-goyim. Paul's "fullness of the Gentiles" uses the same words in Greek.
b: Ephraim did become the leading tribe of the north; prophets often use "Ephraim" as a name for the whole northern kingdom (Isaiah 7:2; Hosea 11:8). Melo haggoyim, "the fullness of the nations," matches word for word the phrase Paul uses in Romans 11:25, to plērōma tōn ethnōn, "the full number of the Gentiles." Some scholars think Paul is consciously echoing this verse, which would connect the scattering of Ephraim among the nations with the ingathering of Gentiles. Others think the match is coincidental.

a: God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh
p: Jewish parents still bless their sons with these words every Sabbath eve.
b: On Friday evening, at the start of the Sabbath, many Jewish parents lay their hands on their sons' heads and say, "May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh" (and for daughters, "like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah"), followed by the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24–26). Why these two and not Abraham or Moses? A common explanation is that they were the first brothers in Genesis who did not fight, even when the younger was put first, and that they grew up in Egypt yet stayed loyal to their father's faith.

a: one shoulder of land
p: The Hebrew shekhem means "shoulder" and is also the name of the city of Shechem.
b: Shekhem echad means "one shoulder," probably a ridge or portion of land, and it is also the name Shechem. Joseph's bones were later buried at Shechem in the plot Jacob had bought (Joshua 24:32; 33:19), and John 4:5 mentions "the plot of ground Jacob gave to his son Joseph." But Jacob "took" this land "with my sword and my bow," though in 33:19 he bought land at Shechem and in chapter 34 he condemned his sons' violence there. Targum Onkelos and Rashi soften it: "with my prayer and my petition." Critical scholars suspect a separate tradition of conquest at Shechem.

a: what will meet you in the last days
p: Acharit hayyamim can mean "days to come" or, in later books, "the last days."
b: Be'acharit hayyamim literally means "at the end of the days." In early texts it often means simply "in the future, later on" (Numbers 24:14; Deuteronomy 4:30). In the prophets it comes to mean the age when God will set all things right (Isaiah 2:2; Daniel 10:14), and the Septuagint renders it ep' eschatōn tōn hēmerōn, "at the last of the days." The Talmud (Pesachim 56a) says Jacob wanted to reveal the end of days to his sons, but the divine presence left him, and the poem that follows speaks instead of each tribe's future.

a: Assemble and hear, sons of Jacob
t: The Blessing of Jacob: prophecy or tribal poetry?
p: Readers disagree about whether this poem is Jacob's prediction or a collection of later tribal sayings.
b: Traditional view: Jews and Christians have read the chapter as Jacob's prophecy on his deathbed, foretelling the tribes' futures and, in 49:10, the Messiah. Critical view: most scholars see a collection of older tribal sayings, gathered perhaps in the time of the judges or early kings. They point to its archaic Hebrew, and to sayings that fit later tribal history: Simeon and Levi scattered, Judah ruling, Zebulun on the coast, Dan in the north. Many consider it among the oldest poetry in the Bible, with the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) and the Song of Deborah (Judges 5). Moses' blessing of the tribes (Deuteronomy 33) is a parallel poem. Literary readers note that it is less a set of blessings than a verdict on each son's character. The earliest retellings already treat it as prophecy: Jubilees 45 has Jacob tell his sons what will befall them, and the Testament of Judah (22–24) promises that Judah's rule will last until salvation comes and pictures a messianic star from Jacob.

a: the first fruit of my manhood
p: As firstborn, Reuben should have been first in honor and power. He loses both.
b: Reshit oni, "the first fruit of my strength," is a legal phrase for the firstborn (Deuteronomy 21:17; Psalm 78:51). The poem piles up words for first place, yeter se'et veyeter 'az, "excess of dignity, excess of strength," and then reverses them: "you will not be first" (49:4, al-totar, the same root). 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 explains the outcome: Reuben's birthright went to Joseph's sons, and the leadership to Judah.

a: Boiling over like water
p: The rare word pachaz suggests foaming, reckless water. Translations differ.
b: Pachaz appears only a few times: for reckless, worthless men (Judges 9:4) and for insolent prophets (Zephaniah 3:4). The KJV's "unstable as water" is a reasonable guess; "turbulent," "reckless" or "boiling over" are others. The crime is Reuben's affair with Bilhah, his father's concubine (35:22). The poem suddenly shifts from "you" to "he" ("he went up onto my couch"), as if Jacob turns away from Reuben in disgust. The tribe of Reuben, east of the Jordan, never produced a judge, king or prophet.

a: their blades are tools of violence
p: Mekerotehem, translated "blades," is found only here. Its meaning is a guess.
b: Suggestions for mekherotehem include "their swords" (some connect it with Greek machaira, "knife"), "their plans" or "their pacts" (from a root meaning "to plot"), and "their origins" or "homeland" (from mekhorah, as in Ezekiel 16:3). Rashi takes it as a weapon and adds that the brothers learned violence from Esau. The sense of the line is clear: the two brothers' instruments were "violence" (chamas), the sin that brought the flood (6:11).

a: may my honor never be joined to their assembly
p: The same consonants can be read "my glory" or "my liver," the seat of feeling. The Greek has "liver."
b: Kevodi, "my glory, my honor," may be repointed kevedi, "my liver." In Hebrew poetry the liver, like the heart, stands for the inner self (compare Psalm 16:9 and 57:8, where some read "my liver" for "my glory"). The Septuagint has ta hēpata mou, "my liver." Either way, it parallels "my soul" in the line before: Jacob wants no part, inside or out, in their deeds.

a: at their whim they crippled oxen
p: Cutting oxen's tendons was a way of disabling them. The Latin Bible read "they undermined a wall."
b: To hamstring ('iqqer) an animal was to cut the tendon of its leg so that it could not walk; Joshua and David did this to captured horses (Joshua 11:6; 2 Samuel 8:4). Genesis 34:28 says that at Shechem the brothers took the oxen, not crippled them, which troubles some readers. Targum Onkelos, the Greek versions of Aquila and Symmachus, and the Vulgate read shur, "wall," instead of shor, "ox," which is why the KJV has "they digged down a wall" (see the variant). "At their whim" (birtsonam) means "as they pleased," for no reason but their own will.

a: I will divide them among Jacob
p: Both tribes ended up without territory of their own, but in very different ways.
b: Simeon's land lay inside Judah's (Joshua 19:1–9), and the tribe faded from history; Moses' blessing does not even mention it (Deuteronomy 33). Levi received no territory but 48 towns spread throughout Israel (Joshua 21) because it became the priestly tribe after its zeal at Sinai (Exodus 32:26–29; Deuteronomy 33:8–11). Rashi explains how the scattering worked out: the scribes and teachers of children came from Simeon, and the Levites went round the threshing floors collecting tithes, so both tribes were spread among all the others. The curse falls on their anger, not on the men themselves.

a: Judah, your brothers will praise you
p: "Judah" sounds like the Hebrew for "praise." The poem plays on the name.
b: Yehudah, attah yodukha achekha: "Judah, you, your brothers will praise you." Leah named him with the same word: "This time I will praise the LORD" (29:35). The word "Jew" comes from Judah's name, and Paul plays on it: a true Jew is one whose "praise comes not from human beings but from God" (Romans 2:29). The bowing of "your father's sons" recalls Joseph's dreams, but here the bowing is to Judah. Genesis gives the family two leaders: Joseph for this generation, Judah for the future.

a: Judah is a lion's cub
p: The lion became Judah's emblem, and Revelation calls Christ "the Lion of the tribe of Judah."
b: Judah is pictured as a young lion that has eaten its prey and lies down, so dangerous that no one dares disturb it. Balaam repeats the lines about Israel as a whole (Numbers 23:24; 24:9). Revelation 5:5 calls the risen Christ "the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David," who turns out to be a slain Lamb. The lion of Judah later became a symbol of Jerusalem and of Ethiopia's royal house, which claimed descent from Solomon. "You have come up from the prey, my son" may also allude to Judah's part in Joseph's story, as Rashi suggests: he "went up" from the suspicion of 37:33.

a: The scepter will not leave Judah
p: Both words name a ruler's rod. Judah's line will keep royal authority.
b: Shevet means "rod, scepter," and also "tribe." Mechoqeq means "one who decrees," and so "lawgiver" (KJV), but in parallel with scepter it means the ruler's staff (as in Numbers 21:18; Psalm 60:7). Ancient art shows kings seated with a staff standing between their feet. The Septuagint takes "between his feet" as a polite way of saying "from his loins" ("a leader from his thighs"), meaning Judah's descendants. Judah's staff was the one Tamar held as a pledge (38:18). The promise is fulfilled in David and his royal line (2 Samuel 7:12–16).

a: Shiloh
p: One of the most debated lines in the Bible. Jews and Christians both read it of the Messiah, with opposite conclusions.
b: Messianic readings. All three Aramaic Targums read "until the Messiah comes, to whom the kingdom belongs"; the Talmud lists Shiloh among the Messiah's names (Sanhedrin 98b); and a Dead Sea Scrolls commentary (4Q252) speaks of "the Messiah of righteousness, the branch of David." The Christian argument. Justin Martyr and Augustine argued that the scepter left Judah when Herod, an Idumean, ruled under Rome, just as Jesus was born. Jewish answers. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 5a) says the scepter never departed: it is the exilarchs who ruled Jews in Babylon, and the staff is Hillel's descendants who taught Torah. Nachmanides, at the Barcelona Disputation (1263), argued that kingship had already left Judah when Zedekiah was taken to Babylon in 586 BC and that the Hasmonean kings were priests, so the Christian argument proves too much: the verse promises only that the kingship will not leave Judah for good. Others note that "until" need not mark an end (compare 28:15). Other readings: "until he comes to Shiloh," the sanctuary town (1 Samuel 1:3); "until tribute comes to him" (Moran). See the variant.
r: Ezekiel 21:27; Numbers 24:17; 1 Samuel 1:3; Isaiah 11:1–10; Hebrews 7:14; Revelation 5:5

a: and to him the peoples will give obedience
p: Judah's ruler will receive the loyalty not only of Israel's tribes but of "peoples."
b: Yiqqehat, "obedience," is a rare word, found otherwise only in Proverbs 30:17. "Peoples" ('ammim) can mean the tribes or the nations. The Septuagint reads "and he will be the expectation of nations," which Christian writers quoted often. The hope of a king from Judah whose rule reaches the nations is developed in Psalm 2:8, Psalm 72:8–11 and Isaiah 11:10, which Paul quotes for the Gentiles' hope in Christ (Romans 15:12).

a: He ties his donkey to the vine
p: A picture of overflowing plenty, later linked with a king riding a donkey into Jerusalem.
b: Vines are so plentiful in Judah's land that a man ties his donkey to the best vine without caring what it eats, and wine is so abundant he could wash clothes in it. Judah's hills were famous vineyard country. The "donkey's colt" returns in Zechariah 9:9, "your king is coming to you... rides on a donkey, on a young male donkey, the foal of a she-donkey," which the Gospels see fulfilled when Jesus enters Jerusalem (Matthew 21:2–7; John 12:14–15). "The blood of grapes" and garments stained red appear again in the image of the divine warrior (Isaiah 63:1–3; Revelation 19:13). Justin Martyr connected these lines to Christ's entry and his blood.
r: Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:2–7; John 12:14–15; Isaiah 63:1–3; Revelation 19:13; Deuteronomy 32:14

a: His eyes are dark from wine
p: The Hebrew can mean "darker than wine" or "dark from wine." Both readings are old.
b: The preposition min can mean "from" or "more than." "Dark from wine" pictures a man who drinks deeply from his abundance; "darker than wine" describes his beauty. Chakhlili ("dark" or "dull") appears also in Proverbs 23:29, of the eyes of drunkards, which suggests that "from wine" is right. Targum Onkelos turns the whole verse into a description of Judah's land: its mountains red with vineyards, its valleys white with grain and flocks.

a: Zebulun will live by the shore of the seas
p: Joshua's boundaries leave Zebulun inland. The poem may reflect a time when it reached the coast or worked its ports.
b: Joshua 19:10–16 places Zebulun in lower Galilee, between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean, without a clear coastline. Some scholars think the tribe worked in the coastal ports of the Phoenicians (the land of Sidon); Deuteronomy 33:19 says Zebulun and Issachar "draw from the wealth of the seas." Traditional readers take it as a prophecy of the tribe's trade. Jewish tradition says Zebulun traded at sea and supported Issachar, who studied Torah (Rashi). Matthew 4:13–16 quotes Isaiah 9:1 about "the land of Zebulun... the way of the sea" where Jesus began preaching.

a: stretched out between the two folds
p: The rare word mishpetayim may mean sheepfolds, saddlebags or hearths. The donkey is lying down at rest.
b: Mishpetayim appears also in Judges 5:16 ("Why did you stay sitting between the saddlebags?", where the Plain chooses "saddlebags") and Psalm 68:13. Suggestions include "sheepfolds," "saddlebags" (the two loads hanging on a donkey's sides), and "ash heaps" or "hearths." "Strong-boned donkey," literally "donkey of bone," means a strong work animal. Issachar's name contains the word sakhar, "wages, hire" (30:18), which fits the next verse. The Septuagint reads the consonants differently: "Issachar desired the good."

a: became a slave at forced labor
p: A letter from about 1350 BC mentions forced laborers working in the area that later belonged to Issachar.
b: Mas 'oved is the term for forced labor gangs, used of conquered peoples under Israel (Joshua 16:10; 1 Kings 9:21). In one of the Amarna letters (EA 365, about 1350 BC), Biridiya, the ruler of Megiddo, says he alone sent corvée workers to cultivate fields at Shunem, a town later in Issachar's territory (Joshua 19:18). Some scholars have suggested that Issachar's people first lived as hired laborers for Canaanite cities, which would match the name ("man of hire") and this saying. The suggestion is attractive but unproven.

a: Dan will judge his people
p: Dan's name means "he judged." The saying plays on it.
b: Dan yadin 'ammo, "Dan will judge his people." Rachel named Bilhah's son Dan because "God has judged for me" (30:6). Dan was a small tribe that later moved north (Judges 18), but it produced one of Israel's best-known judges, Samson (Judges 13:2). "As one of the tribes of Israel" means that a son of a servant wife would have equal standing.

a: May Dan be a snake on the road
p: A small tribe that strikes from ambush. Christian tradition later linked Dan with the Antichrist.
b: A snake that bites a horse's heel and throws a rider suggests a small tribe defeating larger forces by cunning, like Dan's surprise attack on Laish (Judges 18:27) or Samson's lone exploits. Dan also set up an idol shrine (Judges 18:30) and later one of Jeroboam's golden calves (1 Kings 12:29). Irenaeus, noting that Dan is missing from the tribes in Revelation 7:5–8 and reading Jeremiah 8:16, taught that the Antichrist would come from Dan (Against Heresies 5.30.2). Most modern scholars see the saying simply as praise of a small tribe's cunning.

a: I wait for your rescue, O LORD
t: A prayer in the middle of the poem
p: The only line addressed to God, and the only use of "the LORD" in the poem. Why here?
b: This short prayer interrupts the sayings. The word for rescue, yeshu'ah, means salvation or deliverance. The Targums and Rashi explain the placement: Jacob foresaw Samson the Danite, blind and captive, pulling down the Philistine temple (Judges 16:28–30), and prayed, "Not for Samson's rescue do I wait, but for yours, O LORD." Some Christian readers have noted that yeshu'ah is close to the Hebrew form of Jesus' name, Yeshua. Many scholars see a pious response, either Jacob's or a later scribe's, to the danger described in 49:17.

a: Gad: raiders will raid him
p: Four of the six Hebrew words begin with g-d: Gad, gedud, yegudennu, yagud.
b: Gad gedud yegudennu, vehu yagud 'aqev: "Gad, a raiding band will raid him, but he will raid at the heel." The name Gad means "good fortune" (30:11), but here the sound links it to gedud, a raiding party. Gad lived east of the Jordan in Gilead, exposed to raids from Ammonites, Moabites and desert peoples, and its warriors were famed (1 Chronicles 5:18–22; 12:8). The Plain English imitates the repetition with "raiders... raid... raid."

a: he will furnish the dainty food of kings
p: Asher's territory in western Galilee was famous for olive oil and fine produce.
b: Asher's land, in the fertile western Galilee behind the coast, was known for olive oil (Deuteronomy 33:24, "may he dip his foot in oil"), and its produce could well supply a king's table. Asher's name means "happy" (30:13). On the letter that the Hebrew places at the start of this verse, see the variants on 49:19 and 49:20.

a: he gives beautiful words
p: With different vowels, "words of beauty" becomes "lovely fawns," which matches the doe in the first line.
b: The Masoretic vowels read imrei shefer, "words of beauty." A slight change gives immerei shefer or a related word for "lambs" or "fawns": "a doe let loose that bears lovely fawns." Many modern scholars prefer the second as fitting the animal image; others keep the Hebrew. Targum and Midrash connected the "beautiful words" with the song that Deborah and Barak, who came from Naphtali, sang after their victory (Judges 4:6; 5:1), or with Naphtali as a swift messenger bringing good news. The Septuagint has "Naphtali is a stem let loose, giving beauty in its fruit."

a: Joseph is the son of a fruitful tree
p: Ben porat literally means "son of a fruitful one." It may be a tree, a vine, or a young wild donkey.
b: Porat is a form of the root parah, "be fruitful," the root of Ephraim's name (41:52). The usual reading is a fruitful tree or vine by a spring, whose "daughters" (branches) climb over a wall. Some scholars (for example Speiser) read pere', "wild donkey," since other tribes are animals in this poem: "a wild colt by a spring, wild colts on the hillside." The rabbis played on "daughters climbing the wall": Rashi says the young women of Egypt climbed walls to catch sight of Joseph's beauty. The Septuagint reads the whole verse differently: "Joseph is a son increased, my envied son increased, my youngest son, turn back to me."

a: The archers made his life bitter
p: The poem does not say. Readers have named his brothers, Potiphar's wife, or later enemies of the tribe.
b: The "masters of arrows" could be the people who attacked Joseph in his lifetime. Rashi names his brothers and also Potiphar and his wife, whose tongues shot at him like arrows. Critical scholars think the saying refers to the battles of the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, which faced Canaanites and later Arameans. Either way, the next verse turns from the attack to God's help.

a: by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob
t: Names of God in Joseph's blessing
p: Four titles for God come in quick succession: Mighty One of Jacob, Shepherd, Stone of Israel, Almighty.
b: Avir Ya'aqov, "the Mighty One of Jacob," a title found again in Psalm 132:2, 5 and Isaiah 49:26; 60:16 (Isaiah 1:24 has "the Mighty One of Israel"). "Shepherd" recalls 48:15. "Stone of Israel" (even Yisra'el) is unique; it may echo the stone Jacob set up at Bethel (28:18, 22), and it anticipates the frequent title "Rock" for God (Deuteronomy 32:4). "From there" is obscure: it may mean "by the name of" (with a small change of vowels; see the variant) or "from heaven." The Talmud (Sotah 36b) reads "his bow stayed steady" as Joseph's self-control with Potiphar's wife (see 39:11).

a: blessings of breasts and womb
p: Joseph's blessing covers rain from above, springs from below, and children: all of life.
b: The blessings pair heaven and the deep (rain and underground water, compare 7:11) with breasts and womb (children and nursing). There is a play on sound: Shaddai, the Almighty, and shadayim, breasts. Moses' blessing of Joseph repeats much of this language (Deuteronomy 33:13–16). In Canaanite religion such blessings were sought from fertility gods; here every one comes from "the God of your father."

a: on the brow of the one set apart from his brothers
p: Nazir means "consecrated" or "set apart." It is the word behind "Nazirite."
b: Nezir echav can mean "the one set apart from his brothers" (by being sold away) or "the prince among his brothers" (KJV "him that was separate"; Rashi: "separated from his brothers"). The same word names the Nazirite, a person consecrated by a vow (Numbers 6:2), and the noun nezer means a crown. Deuteronomy 33:16 repeats the line. Joseph is both the one who was cut off and the one crowned.

a: Benjamin is a wolf that tears its prey
p: A fierce warrior tribe. Christian writers saw a picture of Saul of Tarsus, a Benjamite.
b: Benjamin was a small but warlike tribe: left-handed slingers (Judges 20:16), the assassin-judge Ehud (Judges 3:15), and Israel's first king, Saul (1 Samuel 9:1–2). Its ferocity nearly destroyed it in civil war (Judges 19–21). The apostle Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin and was named after Saul (Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5). Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.1) read the verse as Paul: in his "morning" he ravaged the church, and in his "evening" he gave out spiritual food. Targum Onkelos linked the verse with the temple altar, which stood in Benjamin's territory, where priests offered sacrifices morning and evening.
r: Judges 3:15; Judges 20:16; 1 Samuel 9:1–2; Acts 8:3; Romans 11:1; Philippians 3:5

a: These are all the tribes of Israel, twelve of them
p: The phrase appears here for the first time. The sons have become tribes.
b: Until now the twelve have been Jacob's sons; the narrator now calls them "the tribes of Israel, twelve of them," the first time the Bible counts the tribes as twelve. Twelve became the number of the whole people of God: twelve stones on the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:21), twelve stones from the Jordan (Joshua 4), Jesus' twelve apostles who will "judge the twelve tribes" (Matthew 19:28), and the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:12). The last line can also be read "each according to his own blessing."
r: Exodus 24:4; Exodus 28:21; Joshua 4:1–9; Matthew 19:28; James 1:1; Revelation 21:12

a: the cave in the field of Machpelah, facing Mamre
p: The family tomb at Hebron, which Abraham bought in chapter 23. A shrine still stands there.
b: Jacob describes the cave in legal detail, repeating the deed of sale in 23:17–20, as if to establish the family's claim. The traditional site is in Hebron, beneath a massive enclosure built by Herod the Great in the first century BC, now the Ibrahimi Mosque and Cave of the Patriarchs, sacred to Jews and Muslims. The enclosure is well preserved; the cave beneath it has been little explored. Jacob alone of the patriarchs dies outside the land, and he is the one who insists most on returning.

a: And there I buried Leah
p: We learn of Leah's death only here. The unloved wife lies beside Jacob; Rachel does not.
b: Genesis never reports Leah's death; we learn only now that Jacob buried her in Machpelah. Rachel, the beloved wife, lies alone by the road near Bethlehem (48:7). Leah, the wife Jacob did not choose (29:30–31), rests with him and with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and her sons Levi and Judah become the priestly and royal tribes. Many readers see quiet justice in this. Rabbinic tradition adds that Adam and Eve were also buried there, which is why Hebron was called Kiriath-arba, "town of four" couples.

a: breathed his last, and was gathered to his people
p: The text says Jacob breathed his last. A rabbinic saying claims he never died.
b: "Gathered to his people" is said of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac and Aaron (25:8, 17; 35:29; Numbers 20:24): it means joining one's ancestors in death. The word "died" (vayyamot), used for Abraham and Isaac, is missing here. The Talmud (Ta'anit 5b) records Rabbi Yohanan's saying, "Jacob our father did not die," explained as meaning that he lives on in his descendants, Israel. Other rabbis objected, pointing to the embalming and burial in chapter 50.

a: to embalm his father
p: Israel's father is mummified in the Egyptian way, one of only two embalmings in the Bible.
b: Only Jacob and Joseph (50:26) are embalmed in the Bible. Egyptian mummification removed the internal organs, dried the body in natron salt for weeks, and wrapped it in linen with resins (like those carried by the Ishmaelites in 37:25). Here physicians do the work rather than the usual priest-embalmers; some suggest Joseph wanted to avoid the religious rites that normally went with it. The practical reason for embalming is clear: the body had to survive a long journey to Canaan.

a: the Egyptians wept for him seventy days
p: Greek writers give similar figures for Egyptian embalming and royal mourning.
b: Herodotus says the body was kept in natron for seventy days (Histories 2.86), and Diodorus of Sicily says Egyptians mourned a dead king for seventy-two days (Library of History 1.72). Egyptian records suggest the full process from death to burial often took about seventy days. Genesis gives forty days for the embalming within a seventy-day period of public mourning, an honor close to that of a king. Israel later mourned Aaron and Moses for thirty days (Numbers 20:29; Deuteronomy 34:8).

a: Joseph spoke to Pharaoh's household
t: Why not speak to Pharaoh himself?
p: The most powerful man in Egypt asks courtiers to speak for him. Perhaps a mourner could not enter the king's presence.
b: Joseph had always spoken to Pharaoh directly. A likely explanation is that, unshaven and in mourning clothes, he could not appear before the king; Esther 4:2 notes that no one in sackcloth could enter the Persian king's gate. Others think Joseph was being cautious, since asking to leave Egypt with his whole family might raise suspicions. He carefully adds, "and I will come back."

a: the one I dug for myself
p: The verb can mean "dug" or "bought." Jacob did not dig Machpelah, but he may have prepared a place in it.
b: Karah usually means "to dig" (as a well, 26:25), but a second verb with the same letters means "to buy" (Deuteronomy 2:6; Hosea 3:2). Rashi gives both. Abraham, not Jacob, bought the cave (23:16–20), so "dug" may mean Jacob prepared his own place inside it. Jacob had also bought land at Shechem (33:19). Joseph phrases the request so that Pharaoh hears of a personal oath and a tomb already prepared.

a: Chariots and horsemen went up with him as well
p: Israel leaves Egypt for Canaan with Egyptian chariots as an honor guard, a peaceful preview of the exodus.
b: The funeral procession brings Jacob's family out of Egypt and back to Canaan escorted by Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen. In Exodus 14:9 Pharaoh's chariots and horsemen will chase Israel, not honor them. The little ones and flocks stay behind in Goshen (50:8), as Pharaoh will later demand (Exodus 10:9–11, 24). Many readers see the journey as a foreshadowing of the greater departure to come.

a: Joseph held seven days of mourning for his father
p: Jewish mourning still keeps seven days, shiva. This is the first seven-day mourning in the Bible.
b: After a death, Jewish mourners observe shiva ("seven"), seven days of mourning at home, receiving comfort from visitors. This verse is the first time the Bible mentions a seven-day period of mourning, and Jewish tradition has always connected the two. Seven days of mourning also appear in 1 Samuel 31:13 and Job 2:13, where Job's friends sit with him seven days in silence.

a: Abel-mizraim
p: The place name is a pun: "meadow of Egypt" sounds like "mourning of Egypt."
b: Abel as a place name usually means "meadow" or "watercourse" (Abel-meholah, Abel-beth-maacah), but it sounds like 'evel, "mourning." The Canaanites see Egyptians mourning, and the name becomes "the mourning of Egypt." The site, "beyond the Jordan," is unknown. "Beyond the Jordan" usually means the east side, which would imply a roundabout route; others think it means the west side from the point of view of a writer east of the river.

a: buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah
p: Genesis buries Jacob at Machpelah. Stephen's speech in Acts mentions a tomb at Shechem.
b: Stephen says that Jacob died in Egypt, "and so did our ancestors. They were moved to Shechem and put in the tomb Abraham had paid silver for, buying it from Hamor's sons at Shechem" (Acts 7:15–16). In Genesis, Abraham bought Machpelah at Hebron (chapter 23), Jacob bought land at Shechem from Hamor (33:19), and Joseph's bones were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). Most commentators think Stephen's speech, as Luke reports it, compresses these traditions into one sentence. Some suggest that "our fathers" means Jacob's sons, not Jacob himself.

a: Suppose Joseph turns hostile toward us
p: Seventeen years after the reunion, the brothers still fear revenge.
b: Esau once planned to kill Jacob after their father's death (27:41). The brothers fear Joseph has been waiting the same way. Their fear shows how hard it is to believe in forgiveness after deep wrong. The verb satam, "hold a grudge," is the one used for Esau's hatred (27:41). Joseph's tears in 50:17 suggest he is hurt that they still doubt him.

a: Before he died your father gave this command
p: Genesis never records Jacob giving this message. The rabbis said the brothers changed the truth for the sake of peace.
b: We never hear Jacob say these words, and he gave his sons detailed last instructions (49:29–33) without mentioning it. Rashi, following the Talmud (Yevamot 65b), says the brothers made it up, and the Talmud draws a rule from the verse: "It is permitted to alter the truth for the sake of peace." Some modern readers think Jacob may really have said it; others see the brothers still unable to approach Joseph directly. The narrator does not decide.

a: Please, forgive the crime of your brothers and their sin
p: The clearest request in Genesis for one person to forgive another.
b: Sa na, "please lift" or "carry," is the Hebrew idiom for forgiving: to lift away a sin (compare Exodus 32:32; Psalm 32:1). The brothers use three words for wrongdoing: pesha' (crime, rebellion), chatta't (sin) and ra'ah (evil). Their appeal to "the God of your father" places them with Joseph under the same God. The verb also echoes Jacob's own fear of Esau: "Maybe he will lift up my face" (32:20), that is, accept me.
orig: שָׂא נָא לְפֶשַׁע אַחֶיךָ (sa na lefesha' achekha)

a: fell down before him
p: The brothers fall before Joseph and offer to be his slaves, the final fulfillment of the dreams.
b: The brothers "fell before him," the last bowing in the story (37:7–10; 42:6; 43:26; 44:14). They offer to be what they made him: a slave. Judah had made the same offer in 44:16. Joseph refuses the position they offer him, which is God's alone (50:19).

a: Am I in God's place?
t: "Am I in the place of God?"
p: Joseph uses exactly the words his father once said to his mother Rachel.
b: Hatachat Elohim ani? Jacob said these words in anger to Rachel when she demanded children: "Am I in the place of God, who has kept the fruit of the womb from you?" (30:2). Now Rachel's son says them to comfort his brothers: judgment and revenge belong to God, not to him. Paul writes, "Never take revenge... leave room for God's wrath, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay'" (Romans 12:19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35).

a: You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good
p: The key verse of the Joseph story: human evil and God's good purpose work in the same events.
b: The same verb, chashav, "plan, intend, count," describes both the brothers and God. Joseph does not say God turned evil into good afterward, but that God intended good in the very same act. Christian theology has used the verse to explain how God can be sovereign while people remain responsible, especially for the cross: "handed over by God's set plan... you put him to death" (Acts 2:23; compare Acts 4:27–28; Romans 8:28). Jewish tradition reads it alongside the saying "everything is foreseen, yet freedom is given" (Mishnah Avot 3:15). Some modern readers are uneasy: does this make God the author of evil? Joseph's words do not excuse the brothers; he calls their plan evil.
orig: אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה (attem chashavtem 'alai ra'ah, Elohim chashavah letovah)

a: spoke kindly to them
p: The Hebrew idiom means to speak tenderly, to comfort and reassure.
b: Vaydabber 'al-libbam, "he spoke to their heart." The same words describe Shechem speaking tenderly to Dinah (34:3), Boaz to Ruth (Ruth 2:13), and God to his people: "Comfort, comfort my people... speak to the heart of Jerusalem" (Isaiah 40:1–2; compare Hosea 2:14). The story that began with brothers who "could not speak to him in peace" (37:4) ends with Joseph speaking to their hearts.

a: Joseph reached one hundred and ten years
p: In Egypt, 110 years was the ideal length of a blessed life.
b: Egyptian texts repeatedly name 110 years as the perfect life span. The sage Ptahhotep says he reached 110 years, and the famous official Amenhotep son of Hapu prayed to reach it. Joshua also dies at 110 (Joshua 24:29). Joseph dies younger than his father (147) and grandfather (180), but at the age an Egyptian would call perfect, a final touch of the Egyptian setting.

a: were also born on Joseph's knees
p: The phrase suggests Joseph adopted or formally accepted Machir's children.
b: "Born on the knees" is the adoption gesture of 30:3 and 48:12. Machir, son of Manasseh, became a leading clan in Gilead and is named in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:14; Numbers 32:39–40). Living to see great-grandchildren was a sign of blessing (Psalm 128:6; Job 42:16).

a: God will surely come to help you
p: Joseph's last promise uses a doubled verb, paqod yifqod. In Exodus it becomes the password of rescue.
b: Paqod yifqod means "he will surely attend to you," come to see and act. God "attended to" Sarah (21:1). In Exodus, God tells Moses to say, "I have surely come to help you, and I have taken note of what is being done to you" (Exodus 3:16), and when the elders hear it, they believe (Exodus 4:31). The Midrash (Exodus Rabbah) says Israel had a tradition from Joseph that whoever came saying these words would be their redeemer. Joseph's promise names all three patriarchs and the land sworn to them.

a: carry my bones up from here
p: Joseph asks to be buried in Canaan. Moses and Joshua keep the promise centuries later.
b: Joseph, the most Egyptian of the patriarchs, refuses to stay in Egypt even in death. When Israel left Egypt, "Moses took Joseph's bones with him" (Exodus 13:19), quoting this verse, and they were buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32). Hebrews 11:22 counts it as faith: "By faith Joseph, when he was dying, spoke of the going out of the sons of Israel and gave instructions about his bones." A traditional Joseph's Tomb stands at Nablus (ancient Shechem).

a: he was laid in a coffin in Egypt
p: Genesis ends in Egypt, with a body in a box. The Hebrew word for coffin, aron, is the word for the ark.
b: Aron means a chest or box; it is the word for the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:10). The Talmud (Sotah 13a) and the Mekhilta picture two chests traveling through the wilderness side by side, Joseph's coffin and the ark, and explain: "This one kept what is written in that one." Genesis began with God's life-giving word over creation and ends with "in Egypt," waiting: the promise of the land is still unfulfilled, and Joseph's coffin is the pledge of the exodus.

a: He was at Kezib
p: The Hebrew says only "and he was at Kezib." The Greek says "she."
b: The Hebrew reads vehayah vikhziv, "and he was at Kezib," without naming the subject; most readers take it to be Judah, away from home when his third son was born. The Septuagint reads "she was in Chasbi." Kezib is probably Achzib in the Judean foothills (Joshua 15:44; Micah 1:14). The name sounds like kazav, "lie, deception," and Micah puns on it; some readers hear a hint of the deceptions to come in this chapter.

a: Pharaoh told them his dream
p: The Hebrew says "his dream" (singular), then "interpret them" (plural).
b: Pharaoh has had two dreams (41:1–7), yet the Hebrew says he told them "his dream," and that no one could interpret "them." The singular treats the two as one message, which is exactly what Joseph will say: "Pharaoh's dreams are one" (41:25). The Plain English keeps "his dream" and smooths the plural pronoun.

a: Pharaoh said to Joseph
t: A different order in the Greek
p: The Septuagint arranges 47:5–6 differently and adds a sentence.
b: In the Septuagint, Pharaoh first tells the brothers' request to settle in Goshen and to make able men overseers of his cattle; then comes a sentence not in the Hebrew, roughly "Jacob and his sons came into Egypt to Joseph, and Pharaoh king of Egypt heard of it"; only then does Pharaoh tell Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you." The change smooths the order of events, and John W. Wevers discusses it in his notes on the Greek Genesis. I was not able to check the Greek wording against a critical edition, so the details here are approximate.

a: The sons of Benjamin
p: Ten sons for the youngest brother is surprising, and the Greek rearranges them.
b: Benjamin, the youngest, has ten sons in this list, more than any brother. Numbers 26:38–40 and 1 Chronicles 8:1–4 list Benjamin's family differently, with some of these names as grandsons. The Septuagint also gives Benjamin only three sons here and makes the rest his grandsons and a great-grandson, which changes the count of Rachel's line discussed at 46:15–27. Like the Hebrew list, the Greek seems to record the founding clans of the tribe rather than one generation. I have not checked the exact Greek name forms.
